The same rank-floored $1/12$ spectral exports achieve substantial token-throughput gains on both AMD and NVIDIA GPUs.
author: Shenghui Li, Thiemo Voigt

title: Does Random Search Discover Task Experts? Revisiting Neural Thickets
content:
arXiv:2611.01262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pretrained models are typically viewed as generalists, requiring bespoke post-training to achieve task-specific expertise. Gan & Isola (2026) recently proposed a striking alternative: that pretrained models lie in a dense neural thicket of task specialists, which can be surfaced with simple Gaussian weight perturbations. We examine this neural thicket of task-specific experts and identify several key findings that question this perspective. First, we find that the apparent lift of the best-of-N selected perturbation decays quickly with selection-set size m, strongly suggesting overfitting to the selection questions. In fact, for 10 of the 12 model-task pairs we study, a simple null model of pure selection noise predicts more than 75 percent of the top expert's reward lift. Second, the top experts' advantage often vanishes on held-out questions or remains within the run-to-run variability of the unperturbed pretrained model. Third, we find that majority voting over the top-K selected perturbations, termed RandOpt(N, K) by Gan & Isola (2026), is often matched or outperformed by majority voting over K samples from the base model. Overall, our results suggest that random weight perturbations may be ineffective at uncovering task experts around pretrained models, and that task adaptation requires more sophistication than random search. Code and artifacts are available at github.com/asil012/RevisitingNeuralThickets.
author: Julian Asilis, Guanzhe Hong, Vatsal Sharan

title: Learning momenta for Hamiltonian-based models
content:
arXiv:2611.01269v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: There has been increasing interest in methodologies that incorporate physics priors into neural network architectures to enhance their modeling capabilities. Among these methodologies, Hamiltonian neural networks (HNNs) and their variants have gained considerable attention. These architectures explicitly encode Hamiltonian mechanics both in their structure and loss function, resulting in desirable properties and additional modeled information. A crucial limitation of HNNs is their reliance on data on the target system's generalized momenta. This severely hampers their applicability when the analytical form of the generalized momenta is unknown, which frequently is the case in real-world applications. The goal of the present work is to develop a general extension of Hamiltonian-based architectures that addresses this issue by simultaneously learning the system's generalized momenta, Hamiltonian structure, and dynamics from data. The proposed architecture learns the generalized momenta when their analytical form is unknown, and only (potentially non-sequential) data on the state and its derivatives is available. A dissipative mass-spring system, a double pendulum, and a rolling disk under nonholonomic constraints are considered as canonical examples to assess the performance of the proposed architecture.
author: Ignacio Puiggros T., A. Srikantha Phani

title: Geometry of Confabulation and Refusal in Small Language Models
content:
arXiv:2611.01272v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Faced with an unanswerable question, small language models can either refuse or confabulate: confidently produce a wrong answer. Can the hidden state before the first generated token provide a clue? Can we flip confabulations into refusals? I introduce ConfabQA, a 784-item benchmark whose obscure-pre-cutoff category breaks the typical correctness/knowledge-cutoff confound and map the geometry of the hidden state with linear probes, a sparse autoencoder (SAE), and direct optimization of intervention directions. On Qwen3-1.7B and Gemma 2 2B the probe separates upcoming refusals from confabulations well beyond prompt features (+7.4/+16.3 pp); on Llama 3.2 3B the ConfabQA margin is within fold-to-fold spread, but a direct refusal probe on PopQA and TriviaQA recovers +18-25 pp. On Qwen I closely inspect three candidate directions for the refusal vector: probe-recovered, Qwen-Scope SAE feature, and directly optimized. Although the three directions are pairwise 50-81 degrees apart, a push at or below the state's own norm along any of them flips most confabulations into refusal openings dominated by the "As..." family. Forcing the opener without touching the hidden state yields the same one-in-three judged-refusal rate as any push. The opposite push collapses refusals mostly into confabulations, yet leaves originally correct answers intact, so the direction gates the opening speech act rather than the knowledge behind it. Confabulations do not resolve into a concentrated feature in a dictionary or a token signature on Qwen3-1.7B. Scoring every probe on the margin over the strongest of four prompt-feature baselines extracts the hidden state's own contribution. Correctness signal is model-dependent and portable only for Llama 3.2 3B: 81% of the probe's margin over test majority survives transfer between ConfabQA, PopQA, and TriviaQA. Benchmark, judge, and code are released.
author: Vladimir Kazei

title: Best-of-Both-Worlds FTRL for Linear Bandits: The Interplay of Information Acquisition, Corruption, and Geometry
content:
arXiv:2611.01299v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study \textit{best-of-both-worlds} (BOBW) algorithms for linear bandits, which aim to simultaneously guarantee $\gO(\sqrt T)$ regret in the adversarial regime and $\gO(\log T)$ regret in the stochastic regime over $T$ rounds. For finite action sets, we introduce \emph{information-acquisition follow-the-regularized-leader} (\IAFTRL{}), the first BOBW algorithm based purely on the follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL) framework that attains an $\gO(\cstar\log T)$-type regret in the stochastic regime, where $\cstar$ is the information-acquisition complexity that characterizes instance-dependent optimality in linear bandits, while retaining the $\gO(\sqrt{T})$ regret guarantee in the adversarial regime. This resolves the open problem posed in~\cite{LeeEtAl2021,KongZ023,ItoT23,ZhaoItoLi2025}.
author: Canzhe Zhao, Vincent Y. F. Tan

title: Accelerating posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with diffusion models: an online-offline perspective
content:
arXiv:2611.01300v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bayesian inverse problems require both informative prior models and computationally feasible posterior inference. Score-based diffusion models provide expressive learned priors, but their use for inversion introduces a conditioning problem: the score of a noised posterior is generally unavailable from a prior score alone. This selective survey reviews the principal approaches to that problem, including likelihood guidance, spectral and projection methods, sequential Monte Carlo corrections, and amortized conditional training. We organize methods by how they split cost between offline preparation and online inference, and compare their assumptions, advantages and limitations, with emphasis on computational speedups. Some ongoing directions and open questions are gathered at the end.
author: Duc-Lam Duong

title: When Does Exploration Prevent Collapse? Three Regimes and the Path of the Reward in Self-Consistency Training
content:
arXiv:2611.01307v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a model without labels by rewarding answers that agree with the majority, but it collapses the policy onto its majority answer and can remove the correct answer from the samples. Exploration can prevent this collapse, yet its strength is chosen by trial and error, and how the training algorithm changes the required strength is unclear. We model training on a single problem as a continuous flow of the logits of a softmax policy and analyze which policies are stable as the exploration coefficient varies. Only collapsed policies are stable below a lower boundary and only policies spread over many answers above an upper boundary, and we derive these boundaries in closed form for an agreement reward with smoothing toward the uniform policy, compute them for the majority reward of TTRL on policies with one leading answer and bound them with interval arithmetic for actions on ordered bins. We prove that under exact gradients, the learning rate and, in a mean-field model, the normalization of GRPO leave these boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through them together with the reward but shift them when exploration bypasses them. Exact sums on these policies then show that a bonus for rare answers needs a coefficient above $1/\log(G-1)$ for groups of $G$ samples before the normalization and about two to three times that after it. In free-form TTRL on MATH-500, a bonus placed before the normalization prevented collapse and kept more correct answers among the samples, although it lowered pass@1.
author: Jaeho Hwang, Uiwon Hwang

title: AgentCBO: Causal Belief Routing for Bayesian Optimization under Unknown Graphs
content:
arXiv:2611.01317v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Causal Bayesian optimization (CBO) typically relies on the unrealistic assumption of a perfectly known causal graph. Recent methods relax this constraint by coupling optimization with structure learning, but they often waste sample budgets on structural uncertainties that are irrelevant to the optimizer. In this paper, we formalize routing-equivalence to shift the objective from full causal-graph recovery to causal belief routing, where structural differences only matter when they alter optimizer-facing objects such as admissible exploration sets and do-priors. Furthermore, we propose agentcbo, a graph-belief routing framework that incorporates LLM causal priors through guarded proposal and commit mechanisms. Specifically, a Language-Prior Agent combines LLM beliefs with constraint-based discovery to extract a protected causal backbone alongside residual uncertain edges. A Calibration Agent and a Residual Repair Agent then refine only these uncertain structures through score-gated bounded local edits. Finally, a deterministic commit gate evaluates candidate updates using routing-proxy checks before allowing them to influence intervention selection. Across ten benchmarks, agentcbo performs comparably to known-graph CBO, demonstrating that guarded LLM priors can improve fixed-budget CBO performance.
author: Qiyu Wei, Xin Zhang, Richard Allmendinger, Mauricio A \'Alvarez

title: Inferring missing locations in human mobility data using memory effects
content:
arXiv:2611.01319v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Empirical datasets used to characterize human mobility are sparse in space and time, owing to technological factors such as coverage and battery, or to the erratic nature of online interactions. Missing data can bias the conclusions drawn from them, so filling the gaps in incomplete timelines is a key challenge in computational social science. Here, we propose a simple imputation method in which the informativeness of an observation decays with its bidirectional temporal distance from the missing entry, at a rate set by a single parameter per individual. On synthetic and real Twitter data, a power-law decay, selected by Bayesian model comparison, yields accurate imputations (macro-AUROC above 0.9 overall, and above 0.8 for the most mobile users) and matches a gap-aware continuous-time Markov chain, outperforming it among the most mobile users. The method is robust to moderate noise and generalizes across countries and European administrative regions.
author: Pablo Rosillo-Rodes, Ant\`onia Tugores, David S\'anchez, Jos\'e J. Ramasco

title: Alignment Flywheel-Guided Suppression Patching for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning
content:
arXiv:2611.01322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learned reward models allow reinforcement-learning agents to use demonstrations, implicit feedback, safety constraints, social norms, or other sources that do not provide a complete hand-designed scalar reward. However, a learned reward model can assign high reward to unwanted behavior. A policy can exploit these errors during training. Later requirements can also identify additional regions where the deployed reward should change. We introduce \emph{flywheel-guided patching}, a mechanism for making such localized corrections without retraining the learned evaluator. An Alignment Flywheel identifies overgeneralized or constraint-violating regions and compiles verified findings into suppression patches. We instantiate the mechanism for Interactionless Inverse Reinforcement Learning using MoE-GUIDE, placing patches in the model's latent space and retrieving only a small local subset during online reward evaluation. In the main MuJoCo benchmark, we evaluate patching without expert-state reset warm starts. We also test whether operator-specified norms absent from the demonstrations can be compiled into the same reward interface and compare this with enforcing the corresponding rules online. The results show that localized corrective information can modify an existing learned reward without providing a complete replacement reward. Compilation can reuse judgments that are expensive or unavailable during control. Cheap deterministic rules may be simpler to check directly at each step. Code for MoE-GUIDE, Alignment Flywheel, and flywheel patching is at https://github.com/decide-ugent/Alignment-Flywheel.
author: Elias Malomgr\'e, Pieter Simoens

title: Same Function, Different Mechanism: Implementation-Local Geometry Beyond Accuracy
content:
arXiv:2611.01328v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Two models can make exactly the same predictions yet respond differently when their implementations are perturbed. A lookup table can change one case independently; a shared rule couples changes across cases. We compare these mechanisms through an implementation chart: a specified local family of logit perturbations around a fixed predictive distribution. Our main result counts the independent prediction changes allowed by exact finite-group sharing: the active dimension is the number of input-output orbits minus the number of input orbits. For softened modular addition, lookup and shared cyclic charts therefore have ranks $p^2(p-1)$ and $p-1$ despite identical predictions. The classical Fisher pullback connects these dimensions to local KL curvature; mechanism-preserving reparameterizations leave the rank unchanged. We also bound the spectral tail under approximate sharing and separate quadratic rank from higher-order learning coefficients. Trained modular-addition models verify that chart rank is measurable, while controlled compiled transformers distinguish compiler-supported intermediate charts from matched alternatives. Negative controls show where this discrimination fails. The framework evaluates specified mechanism hypotheses; it does not infer a unique mechanism from predictions or predict training dynamics.
author: Miroslav L\v{z}i\v{c}a\v{r} (Mereology Labs)

title: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery
content:
arXiv:2611.01334v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A growing number of agentic pipelines search for governing equations: an agent proposes laws and a verifier checks them against simulated trajectories. The verifier sees only a numerical summary: integrals against test functions on a time grid. That summary carries its own discretization error, making the verifier part of the simulator. We freeze the trajectory, candidate library, verifier and thresholds, leaving the agent one move: which permitted summary to admit. Without scores or language models, finer time grids reduce numerical discrepancies and false library rejections. On PDEBench, the verifier instead accepts equations missing diffusion on score-selected summaries. Maximizing a public score rewarding decisive verdicts and larger mismatches when rejecting the library wrongly rejects all 1,500 in-library cases; retrospectively retuning score constants on a separate bank reduces errors to 13/180 at best. We call this evidence-view gaming: reward hacking by choice of permitted summary. In single-turn forced-choice tests, Claude models rarely choose summaries giving wrong verdicts when asked to be accurate, but often do so when asked to maximize the score or report missing physics. In separate trust prompts, they often rank those harmful summaries least trustworthy. Requiring several summaries to agree reduces errors but often withholds a verdict and performs worse than a fixed fine view on PDEBench: a safeguard, not a certificate. Evidence chosen after its verdict is known cannot alone authorize a claim.
author: Orestis Oikonomou, Bogdan Raonic

title: Profile-aware diagnostics of discarded parameter-Hessian mass
content:
arXiv:2611.01335v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A discarded parameter-Hessian fraction depends on the diagonal profile and parameter partition; it is not the Fisher information discarded by K-FAC. We compare off-block squared Frobenius mass with group-size and measured diagonal-profile references at specified weights, inputs and coordinates. Similar initial fractions in ResNet-18 and its skip-free twin accompany different profiles. On the same saved trained ResNet-18 states, changing from stage groups to layers moves estimated mass from below to above the profile envelope. An approximate joint conditional Monte Carlo screen resolves this crossing in 6/6 seed/input cells; the skip-free network has 2 resolved and 4 unresolved comparisons. A separate comparison of nine saved states under two geometry draws splits the full model residual into off-group Hessian action and its remainder: gradient, within-group action and damping. At unit correction scale, off-group input alone increases loss in 17 of 18 state-geometry comparisons; in nine of those cases, the full candidate has lower loss than the remainder-only candidate. After correction-norm matching, seven of the ten comparisons that initially favoured full favour the remainder. These finite-loss contrasts depend on scale and do not establish a restoration benefit.
author: Maxim Bolshim (ITMO University, Saint Petersburg, Russia), Alexander Kugaevskikh (ITMO University, Saint Petersburg, Russia)

title: MoEDDI: Semantic Mixtures of Experts for Long Tailed Drug Drug Interaction Prediction
content:
arXiv:2611.01343v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Descriptor-based drug--drug interaction (DDI) models typically apply a single global predictor despite heterogeneous physicochemical evidence and severely long-tailed labels. We introduce \textbf{MoEDDI (Mixture-of-Experts for Drug--Drug Interaction prediction)}, a chemically organized mixture-of-experts that routes overlapping descriptor families using low-dimensional statistics and combines their sparse top-$2$ mixture with a global T-DDI pathway through a residual logit correction. The residual parameterization can exactly preserve a supplied T-DDI checkpoint at initialization, although the evaluated models are trained from scratch. Across complete test partitions with 178, 86, and 92 classes, MoEDDI improves macro-F1 over reproduced seed-2026 T-DDI baselines from 0.8284 to 0.8485, 0.4729 to 0.6536, and 0.1807 to 0.4671. On the 3,780-feature corpus, the lowest-support group (89 classes with fewer than 50 test examples) shows the largest mean classwise gain (+3.30 F1 points). Calibration improves on one corpus but worsens on two. These single-seed results support semantic conditional specialization while motivating matched ablations and distribution-shift evaluation.
author: Dinh Tan Nguyen, Hien Quang Kha, Minh-Toan Dinh, Xuan-Huy Nguyen, Phu. D Ho, Le Hoang Nguyen, Dang-Manh Ho, Sai Ho Ling

title: Unified dynamics of training, learning, inference, and reinforcement in neural networks
content:
arXiv:2611.01345v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite their remarkable success, neural networks remain largely black boxes, and the mechanisms underlying their behavior are still poorly understood. Nine nanoGPT experiments established training-learning-inference relations: realized updates elicit state-dependent finite-amplitude responses; learning persistently reorganizes distributed functional support, with target-specific readout-boundary crossings determining capability transitions; inference recruits learned support without changing the learned state. Factors identified in the fifth experiment yielded a direct predictor of post-update capability transitions, achieving 91.43% accuracy and 91.49% four-way macro recall across 5,088 targets. We tested these relations and prediction across five additional neural architectures. In a seventh system, concentrated correct feedback eroded previously mastered skills; rebalanced feedback restored their accuracy from 70.31% to 99.48%. Linking inference consequences to subsequent training closes these relations into unified training-learning-inference-reinforcement dynamics.
author: Mian Wang

title: MAPLE: A Multimodal Mobile Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience
content:
arXiv:2611.01351v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Autonomous agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) show great potential in navigating mobile graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to complete complex tasks. However, existing paradigms face fundamental scalability bottlenecks: fine-tuning requires massive high-fidelity datasets or prohibitive training time and compute, while gradient-free approaches rely on custom static heuristics or costly trial-and-error trajectory exploration where feedback is deferred until the end of execution. To address these limitations, we introduce MAPLE (Multimodal Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience), a novel gradient-free multi-agent framework that enables dynamic, step-wise experience sharing and execution-time prompt evolution. Unlike traditional action-reflection architectures that depend on costly, post-hoc self-reflection, MAPLE enables agents to cross-reference and distribute runtime insights in real time at each operational step. This dynamic exchange eliminates blind trial-and-error looping and steers agents along direct, grounded interaction paths. Extensive evaluations on the AndroidWorld and MobileWorld benchmarks demonstrate that MAPLE achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex, long-horizon mobile tasks, while proving scalable and adaptable across novel environments.
author: Jun Wang, Aurora Wei, Lucas Spangher, Ming Zhang, Eugene Ie, Yiannis Kantaros

title: FACET: Feasibility-Automaton Complete Enumeration and Truncation-Free Scoring of Molecular Formulas from MS/MS
content:
arXiv:2611.01352v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Determining the neutral molecular formula of a precursor ion from its tandem mass (MS/MS) spectrum is the first step in identifying an unknown small molecule. Existing methods trade recall, whether the correct formula is among the candidates, against the cost of examining each candidate. Methods that examine each candidate in depth must first shorten the list, by limiting element counts or truncating it, and that is where the correct formula is lost. End-to-end regressors are fast but guarantee neither validity nor recall. We present FACET, which separates deciding which formulas to consider from deciding which one to choose. A feasibility automaton builds a formula one element count at a time and admits exactly the formulas that fit the precursor mass and satisfy the ring-and-double-bond and valence constraints. Run as an exhaustive search, it enumerates the complete feasible set, so every candidate is valid and recall is fixed by the chemical constraints rather than by a trained model. A small neural scoring head then ranks every feasible formula from one pass of a pretrained spectrum encoder, so no candidate is discarded. On the NPLIB1 benchmark FACET reaches top-1 accuracies of $0.859$ with the adduct known and $0.729$ with it unknown, compared with $0.766$ and $0.660$ for the strongest established method, and its recall is the highest. On the external CASMI 2022 set its recall is $1.000$, and with the adduct unknown it is the most accurate of the methods compared.
author: Xujun Che, Depeng Xu, Xiuxia Du

title: Learned Surrogates of Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Turbulence
content:
arXiv:2611.01356v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, the flow of astrophysical and fusion plasmas, is costly to simulate. We present, to our knowledge, the first learned surrogates of three-dimensional resistive MHD turbulence, and compare three standard backbones in that role: a convolutional UNet, a shifted-window transformer and a Fourier neural operator. They are trained as autoregressive emulators of decaying MHD turbulence at a resolution of $128^3$ and Reynolds numbers of 1000, 3000 and 6000, on 500 simulations per Reynolds number, each with one two-stage procedure, single steps and then short rollouts, and stopped by one rule. Over a window of about one large-eddy turnover time, the UNet and the transformer reach relative velocity errors of 0.018 to 0.053 and keep the current sheets, the enstrophy, the current density and the energy spectra of the simulation; which of the two is the more accurate depends on the Reynolds number, the UNet leading at 3000 and 6000 and the transformer at 1000. Applied with the same backbones and training procedure to two public benchmarks, the models reach the lowest error reported to date on the isotropic turbulence set of FactFormer, 39% below the best published model. On the compressible MHD set of The Well, their rollout errors are a third to a half below those of the best of The Well's baselines. They also match a 1.3 B-parameter pretrained foundation model in its rollout windows, with 20-62 times fewer parameters. The code, the configuration of every model, the evaluation scripts and the data generator with the seed of every simulation will be released upon publication.
author: Semih Kacmaz, E. A. Huerta

title: State-Augmented Learning for Post-Deployment Adaptation of Coexisting O-RAN Applications
content:
arXiv:2611.01376v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fixed control policies in Open RAN can require retraining when service requirements, traffic loads, or interacting applications change. We propose ATTUNE, a state-augmented learning method for an energy saving application that coexists with a learned mobility load balancing application under a service constraint. ATTUNE conditions the energy saving policy on a Lagrange multiplier and updates this scalar during operation using measured service degradation, while keeping both applications' network parameters fixed. To train a single policy across service requirements, ATTUNE samples target service levels uniformly and maps them to multipliers through an adaptive table. This procedure accounts for policy-dependent multiplier responses and improves energy savings compared with training over a widened fixed multiplier range. We characterize the induced distribution of service levels and the convergence and fluctuations of the online update. An exact finite-window identity establishes convergence of average measured degradation to the target when the projection corrections vanish on average. Simulations show that a single ATTUNE policy achieves energy savings comparable to policies trained separately for each service requirement. It adapts to changes in the target, load, and partner application without retraining, increases energy savings at light load, and maintains target tracking for separately trained application pairs. No statistically significant increase in cell switching is detected in the evaluated comparisons.
author: Wonhyeok Ko, Yeonseo Jeong, Songnam Hong

title: Toward Executable Multi-framework Front-end Code Generation with Self-Correction
content:
arXiv:2611.01383v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating codes from UI screenshots has recently benefited from MLLMs, yet existing methods centered on HTML targets and transfer poorly to multi-frameworks such as React, Vue, and Angular. However, unlike HTML, which does not entail compilation issues, generating executable code in multi-framework settings is more challenging due to framework-specific differences in syntax and failure modes, as well as the need to maintain global consistency across files. To address this problem, we study executable multi-framework front-end code generation and propose MESCoder, a tree-structured self-corrective generation framework. Our method first extracts a structural scaffold from the screenshot and then constructs sub-trees and assembly relations step by step, transforming large project generation into a sequence of localized decisions. On top of this scaffold, we introduce a unified Project Agent that continuously revises its own partial project under runtime sandbox feedback and dynamically chooses between local repair and cluster level repair. For training, we adopt a two-stage strategy that first initializes the policy offline to learn basic multi-framework generation and repair priors, and then refines it with online reinforcement learning to optimize long horizon executability and final page quality. The resulting framework models multi-framework executability as a conditioned project state transition process and improves the stability and quality of complex front end generation through self correction. Experiments show that our method improves executability, while narrowing the visual-fidelity gap to HTML-based generation. Code is available at https://github.com/leo-lilinxiao/MESCoder.
author: Linxiao Li, Haoran Ma, Chenyue Wang, Jiaye Lin, Haochen Sui, Jiechao Gao

title: ERIA: An Instruction-Optimized Agent for Clinical EEG Reporting
content:
arXiv:2611.01394v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Clinical EEG interpretation requires integrating technical quality, background and behavioral states, interictal and ictal abnormalities, and overall clinical context across long recordings. We introduce ERIA (EEG Reporting and Instruction-Optimized Agent), a locally deployable framework in which a single 27B language-model controller analyzes whole-recording EEGs by orchestrating specialized parametric and signal-processing tools. ERIA combines learned tools for background abnormality, sleep-wake state, seizure-like activity, and interictal epileptiform discharges with deterministic spectral, amplitude, symmetry, montage, and signal-quality analyses. Rather than fine-tuning the controller or using multi-agent orchestration, ERIA keeps the controller weights, specialist tools, and safety constraints fixed and optimizes only its natural-language analysis policy with GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), using feedback from expert-written EEG reports. GEPA improves physician-aligned whole-recording report quality over the raw policy, and the optimized policy transfers to external EEG benchmarks. On CerebraGloss-Bench and BrainBench Foundational Analysis, ERIA remains competitive with the models evaluated in the original benchmarks. These results show that specialist tools and language-level policy optimization can extend the clinical and general EEG capabilities of a single locally executable model while preserving local inference and traceable tool use.
author: Ahmed Sameh, Gayal Kuruppu, Neeraj Wagh, Bridger Brundy, Yogatheesan Varatharajah

title: Sensitivity Inflation from Cross-Record Precision Routing in Private Quantized Fine-Tuning
content:
arXiv:2611.01411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Private fine-tuning of large language models increasingly pairs DP-SGD with low-rank adapters on frozen, quantized backbones, and every such stack inherits one unstated premise: frozen layers keep each record's clipped gradient a function of that record alone. We show that LLM.int8 breaks this premise. It routes outlier activation columns to a higher-precision path using a union over the whole batch, so one record decides how every other record's activations are computed, even though the weights are frozen and the quantization scales are per row. We bound the resulting sensitivity inflation, state a record-isolation contract that restores the standard bound, and define record-owned precision dispatch that meets it with the same GEMMs as batched LLM.int8, so isolation needs no extra arithmetic. We then audit the native CUDA stack (bitsandbytes, PEFT, Opacus) against four matched controls. A constructed LoRA-Opacus witness reaches $15.0\times$ the add/remove bound. On pretrained OPT-125M with natural text, other records alter 20% of record-layer precision splits at batch size 16. An exploratory re-clipping analysis finds 10 of 64 candidate neighbors above the bound once every gradient is clipped; the top pair, revalidated natively, reaches $1.065C$ while every control stays within $C$, and forcing one layer's outlier mask removes the excess. A two-million-draw audit of the released adapters yields $\varepsilon$ lower bounds ($3.25$ at $\delta=10^{-5}$) below the advertised guarantee ($4.38$). Resolving an excess this small at the release level would take about 200 times more draws, whereas checking the sensitivity contract directly exposes it in a few native runs, which makes contract checking the practical audit for private quantized training.
author: Annan Zhang, Shengjie Song, Wenshuai Yao, Lihao Zhang,  Tianmiao

title: Uncertainty-Aware Joint Generative Modeling of Fault Event Sequences and Sensor Time Series in Solar PV Plants
content:
arXiv:2611.01425v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper presents a multimodal generative model designed to simulate a solar energy plant system for predictive maintenance and fault prediction. We propose a novel approach to enhance system generation through conditional generation by leveraging both event sequences and time-series data and improve next event prediction. The framework employs a Transformer Hawkes Process (THP) to encode event data and an iTransformer to encode time-series data, integrated via a co-attention mechanism that effectively captures cross-modal dependencies between discrete events and continuous signals. From these integrated representations, we employ two specialized decoders for simulation: a Conditional Latent Diffusion Model (CLDM) for modeling future sensor trajectories and the Score Matching-based UnceRtainty quantiFication for Transformer Hawkes Process (SMURF-THP) for high-fidelity event prediction. This dual-decoder strategy supports uncertainty-aware, history-conditioned simulation by rolling the model forward for a specified number of generation iterations, producing finite stochastic scenarios rather than deterministic extrapolations over the full observational record. Evaluated on a comprehensive dataset from the Red Rock Solar Site in Arizona, our approach improves aggregate event-prediction F1 relative to baselines and supports applications in predictive maintenance, fault detection, and energy optimization for solar power systems.
author: Jiayu Huang, Boyang Xu, Yongming Liu, Hao Yan

title: When Should an Agent Refresh? Adaptive Index Reuse for Efficient Long-Horizon Reasoning
content:
arXiv:2611.01429v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language agents read code, tool output, and dialogue in contexts that grow at every step. Dynamic sparse attention lets a small indexer choose the earlier tokens each query attends to, but the indexer still scores the whole prefix at every layer. Cross-layer reuse methods such as IndexCache rerun the indexer at only some layers, with one fixed pattern for every input. In an agent, the relevant evidence can change abruptly when a traceback or test result arrives, so fresh selections matter more at some steps than at others. We propose Adaptive Index Reuse (AIR), which keeps IndexCache's execution and learns, for each segment of an agent episode, how many layers refresh their selection. A small controller reads signals from completed computation and the latest tool event, chooses a pattern from a nested library, and learns from terminal task reward under an expected compute budget. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a 128K context, AIR improves success over the strongest static schedule at matched cost on SWE-bench Verified (27.0% to 32.4%), Terminal-Bench 2.0, and three $\tau^2$-bench domains, and it lowers time per successful task on all five. Across 50 backbone, context, and benchmark settings, it matches or exceeds that schedule in 44.
author: Guangyuan Wang, Yifan Zhang, Shilong Liu

title: Correctness and Predictive Uncertainty in Bayesian TSK Fuzzy Regression: A Reproducible Evaluation on Tabular and Building-Meter Data
content:
arXiv:2611.01447v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Uncertainty estimates from fuzzy regression are informative only when the implementation is correct and the comparison protocol makes the sources of variation visible. We revisit a first-order Takagi--Sugeno--Kang (TSK) regression implementation and rebuild its dense, conjugate Bayesian, BIC-based, and rule-level spike-and-slab estimators using corrected code. The corrected pipeline freezes the Gaussian membership partition at training time, uses a scaled conjugate prior, evaluates firing strengths in the log domain, and reports direct posterior-predictive quantiles for Bayesian methods. Across 30 outer 80/20 splits on three targets from two UCI regression datasets, corrected TSK-LS obtains $R^2=0.957$, $0.923$, and $0.786$ on Energy-Heating, Energy-Cooling, and Concrete, respectively; rule-level Gibbs sampling with Bayesian model averaging obtains $0.957$, $0.922$, and $0.784$. We then evaluate the same workflow on a bounded chronological sample of the Building Data Genome 2 meter data that covers 158 buildings across 17 sites. In a common-unit evaluation, every method is scored on the same 47,400 test rows and every trained model uses 94,800 train--validation rows. Persistence has RMSE $27.710$, compared with $29.083$ for both TSK-LS and Bayesian TSK; the pre-specified building-level mean RMSE difference between Bayesian TSK and persistence is $+0.0447$ with a 95% site-cluster bootstrap interval of $[-1.5536,1.5665]$. The Bayesian TSK 90% intervals have PICP $0.980$ and MPIW $116.469$. Taken together, the evidence supports a narrower conclusion: spike-and-slab model averaging is a reproducible implementation option, but it does not provide a demonstrated accuracy or calibration advantage across the tested tabular and building-meter settings.
author: Zhiren Xiao

title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
content:
arXiv:2611.01460v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.
author: Haoyu Zhao, Zafeirios Fountas, Jun Wang

title: Causal Optimal-Transport Attention: Positional Priors and Length Extrapolation
content:
arXiv:2611.01472v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Causal masking obstructs the column balancing used by optimal-transport (OT) attention. We study a prefix-consistent unbalanced operator and characterize the positional prior it induces. Under bounded scores, for any fixed balancing strength $\rho<1$, its fixed point dilutes attention: every fixed window receives a vanishing share as the context grows. For constant scores, we derive an exact scale-invariant prior. We then classify positional encodings by whether their distant attention mass remains bounded away from one. Discrete window-mass bounds quantify the finite-length dilution of summable log-distance priors near exponent one. Preregistered experiments with 25M- and 100M-parameter language models establish improved loss extrapolation over softmax; exploratory comparisons favor an explicit distance bias at a fraction of the cost. CABLE outperforms RoPE with evaluation-time YaRN on every seed at three training lengths. Changing only the bias beyond the training length moves long-context loss in the predicted direction on all 30 tested checkpoints. Even with exponents constrained above one, many heads approach the summability boundary during training. A margin selected by prior-only calculations for a specified window, length range and growth tolerance controls distant-mass growth in the tested setting. These results connect loss extrapolation to positional decay over the lengths actually evaluated.
author: Ming Lian

title: Sweep Less, Steer More: Using Activation Steering Geometry for Reduced Hyperparameter Search
content:
arXiv:2611.01496v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Representation steering methods like difference-in-means (DIM) offer a lightweight approach to controlling LLM behavior, but their effectiveness varies widely across concepts, datasets, and layers, making principled deployment costly without exhaustive hyperparameter sweeps. We build on the discriminability index $d'$, a compute-cheap geometric measure of how well contrastive training activations separate along the steering direction. Across five behaviors on 3 models, we demonstrate uses beyond its established role as a dataset-level steerability predictor. First, in the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) setting, we show that $d'$ reliably identifies performant layers at which to steer, eliminating the need for a layer-wise sweep. Second, we extend this analysis to open-ended multi-token generation, and find that $d'$ remains successful for layer selection across different settings. Lastly, we test whether the position of a generated token's representation on the DIM line predicts steering success on that individual example. In the MCQA setting, this works for high-$d'$ datasets but is inconsistent across behaviors, models, and training-token choices in open-ended generation. This highlights that methods developed and conclusions drawn in single-token MCQA settings do not necessarily transfer to open-ended generation.
author: Nishkal Hundia, Swastik Agrawal, Navita Goyal, Sarah Wiegreffe

title: FedUDG: Federated Domain Generalization with Unlabeled Clients
content:
arXiv:2611.01498v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated domain generalization (FDG) aims to learn models that generalize reliably to out-of-distribution (OOD) environments without centralizing client's data. However, existing FDG methods assume that all source clients have labeled data, limiting their ability to leverage the abundant unlabeled client data available in practice. To address this limitation, we propose FedUDG. At the federation level, FedUDG utilizes a parameter-functional differentiation strategy that maintains a semantic anchor updated solely using ground-truth labels. The remaining parameters absorb knowledge from unlabeled domains under bounded aggregation, preventing domain-biased noise from eroding the class semantics. Within each unlabeled client, FedUDG utilizes a student-teacher framework with two complementary objectives: (1) semantic self-training on high-confidence samples, using the functional differentiation between the semantic anchor and classifier to constrain the model to learn semantically pure and cross-domain stable features; and (2) label-free representation distillation on all unlabeled samples to stabilize learning under appearance variations. Together, these objectives guide the model toward a transferable feature space, while mitigating overfitting to domain-specific characteristics. Furthermore, to address the lack of systematic evaluation of FDG under formal privacy constraints, we develop a sample-level differentially private extension, DP-FedUDG, to quantify the trade-off between privacy and OOD generalization. Across four evaluation protocols, FedUDG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/Jr10426/FedUDG
author: Junyu Ren, Wensheng Gan, Philip S. Yu

title: Improved Sample Complexity Analysis For First Order Bilevel Reinforcement Learning
content:
arXiv:2611.01500v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bilevel reinforcement learning optimizes an upper-level objective through the policy response to a lower-level reinforcement learning problem. Such problems arise when learning a reward model while adapting a policy to that reward. However, a gap remains between sample-complexity guarantees and practical actor--critic training. Tabular analyses restrict applicability to finite spaces, while continuous-state analyses often impose a uniform Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz (PL) condition. We show that this condition need not hold even for smooth positive policies with exactly representable values. We develop a single-loop, fully first-order method for continuous states and finite actions with specified multilayer neural actors and a persistently trained nonlinear critic built from fixed features. Under explicit initialization, regularity, feature-excitation, and value-realizability conditions, fixed reference-KL regularization yields local curvature, and we prove containment of the coupled iterates. Shared trajectories control sampling noise, while paired critic analysis controls normalized critic-error differences as the response perturbation shrinks. A joint descent and tracking argument establishes an improved $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity for $O(\varepsilon)$ expected squared gradient norm of the upper objective induced by the selected regularized policy response, including critic training.
author: Mudit Gaur, Naman Saxena, Vaneet Aggarwal

title: Abstention Spends Its Budget on Local Label Variance More Than on Novelty: Auditing Conformal Calibration and Selective Prediction under Molecular Scaffold Shift
content:
arXiv:2611.01512v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selective prediction with split conformal calibration promises a post-hoc fix for molecular property prediction: abstain on the least reliable compounds, ideally out-of-distribution chemistry, and the retained set becomes trustworthy without retraining. We audit this recipe for a gradient-boosted fingerprint model on lipophilicity (regression) and BBBP (classification) under a Bemis-Murcko scaffold split, holding the fitted model and evaluation molecules fixed while varying only the calibration fold (18 replicates). (i) On lipophilicity, coverage depends on calibration provenance: calibrating on held-out training-scaffold molecules falls below nominal (PICP 0.841 at a 0.90 target), while novel-scaffold calibration recovers it (0.904); on BBBP, coverage stays above nominal in every regime. (ii) For split conformalized quantile regression (CQR) the conformal correction is a constant, so conformalization does not change what is abstained on. (iii) The abstention score (CQR width; effectively ensemble variance on BBBP) tracks local label variance more than chemical novelty: controlling for local label variance largely explains away the novelty association (partial Spearman 0.067 and 0.047). (iv) At a fixed assay budget, gating on interval width or ensemble variance never improves hit precision over ranking by point prediction, at the pre-specified operating point or across 20 exploratory settings; a plain novelty gate shows small, uncorrected gains at the smallest budgets. (v) In an exploratory analysis, exact conformal selection exceeds its false discovery rate target under training-scaffold calibration (0.303 at q=0.2) and is consistent with it under novel-scaffold calibration, contributing a data-driven batch size rather than a better ranking. Conformalization earns its keep through guarantees whose validity hinges on calibration provenance, not by choosing what to abstain on.
author: Arnav Srivastava, Krishna Kassetty

title: InformedXRD: Reproducible Benchmarks and Physics-Informed Evaluation for Powder Diffraction Symmetry Classification
content:
arXiv:2611.01525v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning for powder diffraction (PXRD) symmetry classification is being trained at scale, yet the field lacks a common evaluation standard: papers report results on different subsets of experimental archives, with different target taxonomies, preprocessing, and metrics, and published models are rarely released in a form that permits rescoring. We present InformedXRD, an evaluation framework with three parts: (i) a machine-readable mapping from 230 space groups to 99 extinction groups, the finest classes powder diffraction can identify from systematic absences alone; (ii) a benchmark-construction method whose inclusion rules are specified as code and reproduce from a frozen snapshot, instantiated as RRUFF-473, RRUFF-325, and, as a small example, opXRD-98; (iii) a reporting protocol with prior-only frequency baselines, a label-permutation test, a hierarchy-aware error metric on the condensed translationengleiche subgroup graph, and stratified evaluation. We build on the mapping, RRUFF benchmarks, subgroup graph, and four ViT checkpoints released in our earlier work (Baggett et al., 2026). Using these checkpoints, a 1D residual CNN, and six architectures trained under the XRDBench recipe (Cao et al., 2025), we show that evaluation design changes what conclusions are justified: paired tests point in different directions at Top-1 and Top-5; paired Top-k tests do not separate the three leading XRDBench models, while hierarchy-aware analysis describes error distance and direction across all six; an input-blind frequency predictor matches the models on aggregate Top-k, yet a label-permutation test still detects pattern-specific evidence; and stratified analysis exposes a label-entropy confound that aggregate accuracy hides. All mapping tables, benchmark code, scripts, and checkpoints are released as shared infrastructure for PXRD-ML evaluation.
author: Edward G Friedman, Elizabeth J. Baggett, Abhishek Shetty, Derrick Chan-Sew, Vanellsa Acha, Harshitha Dwaracherla, P. A. Kienzle, William Ratcliff II

title: Learning Gradients of Homogeneous Functions
content:
arXiv:2611.01530v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Homogeneous gradient functions have widespread significance, including applications in maximum energy subspace selection and retrieval problems. Euler's homogeneous function theorem specifies how the potential associated with a positively k-homogeneous gradient field can be recovered directly from the field itself. We use Euler's theorem to build on GradNets and propose a homogeneous gradient network architecture that is guaranteed to correspond to the gradient of a homogeneous function. Then, we describe how monotone homogeneous GradNets universally approximate the gradients of k-homogeneous convex functions. The inductive bias of homogeneous GradNets enables them to outperform baseline ICNNs by up to 7dB in our max energy subspace projection experiment and by up to 13% higher accuracy, 98% fewer parameters, and 70% fewer FLOPS in our amortized inner product search experiment.
author: Mayur S. Gowda, Srinivasa Pranav, Shreyas Chaudhari, Jos\'e M. F. Moura

title: Generative Modeling with Continuous Flows: Sample Complexity of Flow Matching
content:
arXiv:2611.01559v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Flow matching has emerged as a promising alternative to diffusion-based generative modeling, offering a continuous-time ordinary differential equation formulation with fast sampling and a simple regression-based training objective. Despite its empirical success, some theoretical analyses idealize the learning procedure by assuming that the velocity field is obtained by exact empirical risk minimization. This assumption does not reflect the practical finite-dataset setting, where the empirical flow-matching loss is only approximately minimized by a finite number of stochastic-gradient updates. We develop an empirical-risk-minimizer-free analysis for flow matching that explicitly accounts for both finite-sample statistical error and finite-time empirical optimization error. Our analysis considers a finite dataset of \(N\) flow-matching samples and a learned parameter \(\theta_T\) obtained after \(T\) stochastic gradient updates on the empirical objective. Under regularity assumptions on the interpolation path, sub-exponential source and target distributions, approximation by a bounded-parameter smooth neural velocity class, empirical-loss optimization, and uniform flow stability, we prove a guarantee that holds with high probability over the finite training dataset and in expectation over the stochastic-gradient randomness. The resulting bound separates approximation error, statistical error from the finite dataset, tail error from unbounded source and target distributions, and empirical optimization error from approximate minimization of the finite-sample objective.
author: Mudit Gaur, Prashant Trivedi, Shuchin Aeron, Amrit Singh Bedi, George K. Atia, Vaneet Aggarwal

title: Finite-Time Online Sample Complexity for Conditional Diffusion Models
content:
arXiv:2611.01562v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the finite-time training and sampling error of conditional diffusion models trained by online stochastic-gradient denoising score matching. Rather than assuming access to an exact empirical or population risk minimizer, we analyze the score network produced after a finite number of stochastic-gradient updates under an explicit localized Polyak--\L{}ojasiewicz (PL) condition, stochastic-gradient regularity, and a trajectory-containment assumption. Our analysis separates the network approximation complexity from the online training-sample budget and propagates both errors through the reverse diffusion process. Under anisotropic smoothness, a joint intrinsic-dimensional structure for the data and conditioning variables, sub-exponential tails, and explicit approximation-class compatibility, we obtain a conditional score approximation error of order \[ \widetilde{\mathcal O}\!\left(M^{-\eta_{\mathrm{app}}}\right), \qquad \eta_{\mathrm{app}} = \frac{2\alpha_x} {2\alpha_x+d_x'+(\alpha_x/\alpha_y)d_y'}, \] where \(M\) denotes the approximation complexity, \(d_x'\) and \(d_y'\) are the intrinsic response and conditioning dimensions, and \(\alpha_x,\alpha_y\) are their corresponding smoothness exponents. For \(N=RB\) online denoising samples used by SGD, the finite-time optimization error is controlled explicitly in terms of the PL, smoothness, gradient-noise, and initialization constants. Combining these ingredients with reverse-process stability yields a total-variation bound that decomposes into terminal-initialization, time-discretization, approximation/localization, and finite-time optimization errors.
author: Mudit Gaur, Prashant Trivedi, Sasidhar Kunapuli, Amrit Singh Bedi, Vaneet Aggarwal

title: Meta-memorization and memorization scaling laws in transformers
content:
arXiv:2611.01564v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Larger transformers can memorize more data, with a capacity (in bits) that scales roughly linearly with the number of parameters. Counterintuitively, larger models also memorize faster, requiring fewer repetitions of a sequence during training before it is memorized. We reproduce both memorization scaling laws in transformers trained on random binary sequences, showing that rapid memorization can arise even when data contain no semantic or compositional structure. Rapid memorization is due to a meta-memorization effect, where models trained to memorize a large set of random sequences learn to memorize novel sequences more quickly. The rate $r(t)$ at which models memorize grows with training time $t$ as a power-law $r(t) \sim t^{\beta}$ with a fixed exponent $\beta$ but an increasing upper cutoff across model scales. Meta-memorization enables even one-layer transformers to few-shot memorize a 100-bit sequence. This effect is partly explained by the formation of structured attention heads that convey position-invariant sequence information to MLPs where memorized sequences are stored. Meta-memorization is recapitulated in a simplified model of a dense associative memory where retrieval is constrained by an attentional bottleneck. Our results suggest transformers, through pre-training, acquire reusable mechanisms that enable highly efficient storage and retrieval of memories.
author: Alex Nguyen, Kenneth A. Norman, Gautam Reddy

title: Beyond Validation Loss: Coverage and Reliability Dynamics in Robot Policy Pretraining
content:
arXiv:2611.01565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In modern robot learning, generative robot policies are first pretrained through supervised learning from demonstrations, then refined through reinforcement learning, supervised finetuning, or other forms of posttraining. Yet conventional pretraining metrics, such as validation loss and average task success, provide an incomplete account of which policies support both effective direct deployment and subsequent posttraining. In this work, we study closed-loop pass@k, which evaluates the probability that k rollouts from the same initial condition attain at least one success. Thus, pass@1 measures mean task success; large-k pass@k measures whether success remains reachable under repeated sampling. Across a wide range of posttraining recipes, we show that large-k pass@k reveals posttraining differences not captured by pass@1. In particular, checkpoints with similar pass@1 but different large-k pass@k have different posttraining performance. Moreover, we show pass@k peaks at different checkpoints during supervised pretraining, revealing a coverage-reliability tradeoff over the course of training. Based on these observations, we propose two practical interventions: (1) a purely offline checkpoint-selection criterion that balances coverage and reliability without closed-loop evaluation, and (2) a generative data augmentation procedure that expands supervision beyond the finite demonstration set, preserving large-k pass@k while maintaining or improving pass@1 and raising the observed coverage-reliability Pareto frontier. Together, our results motivate evaluation, checkpoint selection, and training procedures that explicitly account for posttraining. Blog post, visualizations, and code are available at https://zhanyisun.github.io/robot-policy-learning-dynamics/.
author: Zhanyi Sun, Max Simchowitz, Shuran Song

title: Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation with Sibling Alignment for Generative Recommendation
content:
arXiv:2611.01568v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generative recommendation retrieves items by autoregressively generating semantic IDs, typically via beam search. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enhances training supervision by transferring privileged self-teacher knowledge at student-generated states. However, beam-search retention depends on competition among prefixes: visited states differ in importance, and initially reliable decisions may approach the pruning boundary as training evolves. Moreover, conventional distribution matching couples target-token confidence with preferences among competing continuations, potentially weakening relational supervision when the self-teacher strongly favors the target. To address these challenges, we propose Search-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (SA-OPSD), a framework that transfers privileged self-teacher knowledge to the states visited during the student's own beam search. Specifically, we introduce Evolving-Boundary Sampling, which prioritizes search-critical states by considering both current pruning-boundary proximity and initial-reference retention-margin decline under a controlled distillation budget. Furthermore, we develop Confidence-Decoupled Branch Distillation, which separates target-probability calibration from informative sibling relations to better preserve the teacher's preferences among competing branches. Experiments on Industrial, Office, and Instruments demonstrate strong performance for SA-OPSD.
author: Rongfeng Guo, Zhuang Zhuang, Ji Dai, Peng Zhao, Shijie Li, Jie Chen, Teng Long, Vincent Tao Hu, Fei Pan

title: Autoencoder Based Deep Clustering of Point Clouds
content:
arXiv:2611.01594v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Motivated by a problem in Generative Specification-Producing AIs (SPAIs), we focus on a problem of deep clustering of three-dimensional shapes specified by point clouds. After reviewing clustering and deep clustering, we study the fully unsupervised pipeline in which a FoldingNet autoencoder is first trained for reconstruction and then K-means++ is then applied to the resulting codewords. We report clustering accuracy (ACC), normalized mutual information (NMI) and adjusted Rand index (ARI) on ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 datasets, as a function of the number of clusters K. We also provide t-SNE visualizations of the codewords, and discuss the choice of K.
author: Nader Alfares, Guangmingmei Yang, David J. Miller, George Kesidis

title: DyRadio: Spatiotemporal Diffusion for Dynamic Radio Map Reconstruction
content:
arXiv:2611.01603v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate radio map (RM) reconstruction is essential for environment-aware wireless networks. Sampling-based methods, which infer radio conditions from sparse measurements, are widely adopted because they do not require explicit knowledge of transmitter configurations. However, in dynamic environments, time-varying propagation conditions cause RMs to evolve, complicating reconstruction from temporally distributed sparse observations. Although cross-frame observations provide complementary spatial information, their direct aggregation can introduce temporal state mismatch. Furthermore, unknown measurement noise adds to the reconstruction difficulties. To address these challenges, we propose DyRadio, a framework that integrates spatiotemporal RM reconstruction with unknown noise estimation. Specifically, a propagation-prior-guided, noise-conditioned spatiotemporal diffusion model (DM) jointly reconstructs consecutive RMs by capturing cross-frame dependencies, while adapting to measurement noise levels. To estimate the noise level, an iterative predictive likelihood method alternates between DM-based blind-area prediction and noise-level updates. The estimated noise level then conditions reconstruction of the complete RM sequence. Experimental results demonstrate superior reconstruction accuracy and robustness against measurement noise, with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) improvements of 1.18-5.75 dB over the best-performing baseline across all evaluated settings.
author: Zhijie Fan, Zhifeng Zhao, Rongpeng Li

title: Sonny-ENS: demystifying machine-learning ensemble weather forecasting
content:
arXiv:2611.01614v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Every weather forecast is uncertain, and decisions from flood warnings to energy trading depend on how well that uncertainty is quantified. Machine-learning (ML) ensembles now quantify it better than the best physics-based ensemble, yet two things about them remain opaque: whether their skill requires hundreds to thousands of accelerator-days of training, and how a network with a simple source of randomness produces a spread that follows the flow. Here we introduce Sonny-ENS, an ensemble of three 68.9-million-parameter networks with Monte Carlo dropout, trained on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in 2.7 A40 GPU-days. On 2022, it has a lower CRPS than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS) on 96% of 570 targets and an 8.3% lower mean CRPS at lead times of 1-10 days. It outperforms the operational GenCast on 69% of the targets, and a 51-member, 15-day forecast takes 69 s on one GPU. Ablations identify the ingredients of this skill, and a Kolmogorov-Arnold sparse autoencoder shows that dropout injects uncertainty mainly in the tropics, whereas the spread grows where the atmosphere is baroclinically unstable (spatial correlation 0.91 with the Eady growth rate). Skillful probabilistic weather forecasts are therefore within reach of a single GPU server.
author: Minjong Cheon

title: LLM-Enhanced Multimodal House Price Prediction using Structured, Textual, and Visual Features
content:
arXiv:2611.01615v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate house price prediction is essential for real estate buyers, sellers, agents, and financial institutions. Traditional methods rely primarily on structured data, e.g., number of bedrooms, bathrooms, parkings, but they overlook rich contextual information embedded in textual descriptions and property photos. Previous deep learning approaches for house price prediction have fused multimodal data but they fall short to extract structured spatio-temporal and contextual features from texts and semantic visual information from images. In this paper, we introduce a novel multimodal framework that addresses these limitations by systematically integrating structured attributes, textual descriptions, and visual images of properties to achieve higher prediction accuracy while maintaining interpretability. We use a large language model to derive domain-specific spatio-temporal and contextual features from text, and an unsupervised vision-language approach to automatically group photos into meaningful classes like indoor, outdoor, mixed, or floorplan, that are commonly present in real-world house listings. These categories are created without manual labeling by aligning image clusters with carefully designed pseudo text prompts. We fuse all features into a unified representation and use an optimized regressor to predict prices. Experiments on a large real-world property dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional methods and existing multimodal baselines. Ablation studies confirm that the novel textual feature extraction and categorized visual embeddings substantially contribute to more accurate and reliable price predictions.
author: Khandokar Md. Rahat Hossain, Souvik Das, Tahsina Hashem, Mohammed Eunus Ali, Tanzima Hashem

title: CREDO: Evidence-Conditioned Credit Assignment for Temporal Reasoning Agents
content:
arXiv:2611.01643v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering (TKGQA) requires language model agents to retrieve evidence, select relevant facts, and perform multi-step temporal reasoning. However, the trajectory-level outcome signal in GRPO does not explicitly distinguish the quality of intermediate decisions: downstream failures can penalize useful evidence acquisition, while identical rewards in all-failed groups eliminate the relative outcome signal despite differences in intermediate progress. We propose Credit Redistribution with Evidence-Driven Opportunities (CREDO), which uses intermediate evidence to recover local supervision, including in all-failed groups, and determine where outcome supervision acts. CREDO assigns positive stage-level credit through comparisons among rollouts of the same question and uses retained answer overlap as an opportunity proxy to shift part of the outcome-policy weight toward reasoning and answering. The framework preserves terminal rewards and trajectory-level advantages, while redistribution conserves total outcome-policy weight per trajectory. Following the public evaluation protocol of prior work, CREDO raises Overall accuracy from 78.0% to 82.4% and Multiple accuracy from 55.0% to 65.6% on MultiTQ relative to the strongest published baseline in our comparison. On TimelineKGQA, it raises cross-KG accuracy from 30.9% to 36.4% relative to our reproduced baseline via direct transfer to ICEWS Actor under matched training and evaluation settings.
author: Yue Leng, Shengtao Wen, Xiang Chen, Xinyi Zeng, Yu Tian, Sheng-Jun Huang

title: Yielding Fairness: Coupled Learning and Fairness for Value-Weighted Ranking
content:
arXiv:2611.01647v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Risk screening and recommendation systems pass or block accounts that generate both value and loss. Under a blocked-value budget, a cap on expected value forgone through blocking, the optimal ranking orders accounts by expected value per unit expected loss, a ratio of conditional expectations. This rule can conflict with accepted harm or net-harm criteria, blocking accounts that another criterion would pass at the same budget. We call these cases account-level objections and define group complaint disparity as the difference between groups' normalized realized objections.
  Weighted binary cross-entropy (W-BCE) implements the value-per-loss order with one score. Objection penalties modify the ranking, while group multipliers scale those penalties differently by group, tracing tradeoffs between loss capture and complaint disparity. This preserves the value-budgeted ranking structure and makes the cost of reducing contestable blocks explicit.
  Across public recommendation, insurance, credit, and mortgage datasets, we compare undamped W-BCE with ordinary BCE using yield Gini, an area summary of loss capture versus blocked value. Logarithmic weight damping is evaluated separately. Held-out evaluations measure capture-disparity tradeoffs. Validation-selected group-aware complaint penalties improve complaint closure in some cohorts. A corrected comparison normalizes and enlarges candidate policy banks using validation-only price sweeps and retains all ten applicable sources. The source-level results do not establish a statistically significant average advantage over group-blind pricing at the fixed minimum retained loss capture. We also compare with blocked-count, blocked-value, and protected-loss parity postprocessors, which do not directly constrain realized objections, and measure objections in candidate-count and loss units.
author: Ami Tavory, Yaniv Sheena, Shaked Bar, Yair Zagdansky

title: Near-Optimal $\sqrt{K}$-Regret for Online Learning in Uninformed Markov Games
content:
arXiv:2611.01649v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study online learning in two-player uninformed Markov games, where the opponent may follow an arbitrary, unknown policy in each episode and the learner does not observe the opponent's actions. [TWYS21] showed that achieving sublinear external regret requires an exponential dependence on the episode length $H$. Motivated by this limitation, they studied the weaker notion of Nash-value regret and obtained an $\widetilde{O}(K^{2/3})$ regret bound, where $K$ is the number of episodes. More recently, [LLZR26] introduced a stronger notion called empirical Nash-value regret and achieved an $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{K})$ bound when the opponent's non-stationarity is moderate, including the case where the opponent follows a fixed policy. However, whether the $\sqrt{K}$ rate is achievable in the worst case remained open.
  In this paper, we resolve this open question by developing an algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{O}(H^{3/2}S\sqrt{AK})$ empirical Nash-value regret against arbitrary opponent policies, where $S$ is the number of states and $A$ is the number of learner's actions. Specifically, our algorithm combines global and local planning by maintaining a collection of candidate predictions of future losses, each associated with a policy. Global planning learns which candidates to favor across episodes, while local planning combines their policies differently at each state to make decisions. A key ingredient is to coordinate these two components to control the discrepancy between local loss estimates and the total loss of the executed policy, using only the learner's observed trajectories.
author: Junyan Liu, Haipeng Luo, Lillian J. Ratliff, Zihan Zhang

title: Physics-Informed One-Step Generation on Long-short flow maps
content:
arXiv:2611.01651v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Physics-informed generative models should produce samples that are both data-aligned and physically valid, yet existing methods are often iterative and too slow for practical use. Achieving this with a one-step flow-map model is difficult because both data-distribution and physics-constraint learning are enforced only indirectly through surrogate objectives, making their joint learning fragile for long-range flow maps. We propose \textbf{Physics-Informed Long-Short Flow Maps with Direct Guidance (LSFM-DG)}, which makes direct target computation feasible by decomposing one-step generation into a long flow map for global evolution and a near-terminal short flow map with computable closed-form solutions and physics potentials. As the short flow map shrinks to zero, it provides both direct distributional and physical targets for learning the long flow map. This yields a unified one-step flow-map model that removes Jensen's gap, improves training stability, and achieves stronger data fidelity and physical consistency without distillation.
author: Zhiqi Li, Duowen Chen, Jinjin He, Bo Zhu

title: A Hybrid Anomaly Detection Method for Electric Vehicle Identification from Smart Meter Recordings
content:
arXiv:2611.01655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In recent years, electric vehicles (EVs) have attracted much attention due to their potential to decarbonize the transport system. EV charging imposes challenges on power grids, such as load imbalance and voltage instability. Therefore, electricity distributors need to identify which users have an EV. Smart meter recordings can be effectively used for this purpose. The major issue associated with such data is the imbalance problem, where the majority of the data belongs to users without EVs. The existing methods for EV identification from smart meter recordings have framed it as a classification task. In this paper, we frame the problem as an unsupervised problem and propose a hybrid anomaly detection method that combines the power of prediction-based and reconstruction-based anomaly detection methods. The proposed model considers temporal and stochastic representation information of smart meter time series via prediction-based and reconstruction-based components, respectively. The performance of the proposed model is compared with state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods. Its superiority is verified on real-world data.
author: Ali Babalhavaeji, Hui Song, Mohammadreza Radmanesh, Mahdi Jalili

title: A Hybrid Anomaly Detection Method for Multivariate Time Series
content:
arXiv:2611.01661v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multivariate time series are ubiquitous in monitoring smart systems such as power plants, smart houses, and servers. These systems use multiple sensors to collect the system's status over time. Those sensors represent the status of the whole system as one entity. Anomaly detection in such smart systems is of critical importance to prevent system failure and maintain functionality. But anomaly detection in such multivariate time series data is very challenging since this type of data includes both temporal and spatial information. Capturing both of these pieces of information is important to detect anomalies. In this paper, we propose a hybrid deep learning-based anomaly detection method, which captures both temporal and spatial information. We propose to take advantage of the feature extraction capabilities of 2d convolutional network in a variational autoencoder, alongside a prediction-based deep neural network of 2d convolutional networks and a gated recurrent unit network to capture both spatial and temporal information. Experiments on public data against state-of-the-art show the potential of our method.
author: Ali Babalhavaeji, Hui Song, Mahdi Jalili

title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
content:
arXiv:2611.01666v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
author: Bowen Xu, Boyu Chen

title: Wave Physics as Representation: Tensor-Structured Neural Reconstruction for Ocean Acoustic Fields
content:
arXiv:2611.01680v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reconstructing three-dimensional (3D) complex ocean acoustic fields from sparse measurements is challenging due to highly oscillatory wave structures and restricted sensing patterns/routes. Learning-based approaches fall into two categories. First, purely data-driven models can learn complex field patterns, but do not explicitly exploit wave physics that may enhance interpretability and reduce training costs. Second, physics-informed methods impose a specified physical equation as a reconstruction constraint, but often require environment-dependent parameters that are difficult to acquire. As a result, practical 3D acoustic field reconstruction that is both physically grounded and robust to uncertain environmental information remains largely unexplored.
