title: 3-D Anisotropic Magnetotelluric Inversion With Cross-Gradient and Anisotropic Constraints on Principal-Axis Resistivities
content: Magnetotellurics (MTs) are widely used for imaging subsurface electrical structures. Because geological formations commonly exhibit electrical anisotropy, arbitrary anisotropic MT inversion is important for reliable subsurface characterization. However, compared with isotropic inversion, it involves more model parameters, resulting in stronger nonuniqueness and reduced inversion stability. To mitigate these challenges, a 3-D arbitrary anisotropic MT inversion method based on the nonlinear conjugate gradient (NLCG) algorithm is developed with principal-axis cross-gradient (PACG) and anisotropy constraints. The PACG constraint promotes structural consistency among the principal-axis resistivity components, whereas the anisotropy constraint regulates their relative magnitudes, providing complementary structural and parameter regularization. The approach is evaluated using synthetic models with increasing structural complexity. Results show that smoothness regularization alone may lead to spurious anomalies and structural distortions. The anisotropy constraint can improve the recovery of principal resistivities and anisotropic parameters in some cases, but its effect depends on model characteristics and geological complexity. In contrast, the PACG more consistently improves spatial structural consistency and suppresses structural distortions and spurious anomalies. Joint application of both constraints generally yields more reasonable target geometries, boundary continuity, and parameter distributions, with improved recovery of horizontal rotation angles in several tested cases. These results demonstrate that the joint constraints provide complementary structural and parametric regularization, helping to mitigate the effects of nonuniqueness and improve the reconstruction of complex anisotropic structures.
author: Shengtao Wang, Changhong Lin, Jiantao Ni, Depeng Zhu, Dongyue Xin

title: Mapping Urban Mixed Land Use via Multimodal Fusion and Large Language Models
content: Accurate mapping of mixed urban land use supports sustainable planning, yet conventional supervised methods are constrained by the semantic gap and the need for extensive labeled data. We develop an interpretable geospatial AI (GeoAI) framework that combines multimodal feature fusion with zero-shot large language model (LLM) inference. Using Beijing and Changsha as test sites, the framework delineates urban parcels from crowdsourced road networks and aligns points of interest (POI) text with geographic coordinates through contrastive learning. The resulting representations are combined with multispectral, 3-D morphological, nighttime-light, and space-syntax features. Hierarchical density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (HDBSCAN) then groups parcels with similar functional profiles, and the LLM assigns cluster-level land-use semantics while preserving soft memberships for mixed-use interpretation. The framework achieved area-weighted OAs of 70.91% in Beijing and 76.90% in Changsha against Essential Urban Land Use Category (EULUC)-China 2.0, and primary-function overall accuracy (OA) of 85.0% and 83.3% in temporally aligned 2024 manual validation. The results show that cluster-level semantic inference can represent urban functional mixtures more transparently than deterministic single-label mapping.
author: Youcheng Song, Chang Xia, Weilin Wang, Haijun Wang, Bin Zhang, Haoran Zeng, Yaotao Liang, Xiaoxu Cao

title: Improving Cloudy-Sky Surface Downward Longwave Radiation Estimation by Separating Cloud and Subcloud Atmospheric Contributions
content: Surface downward longwave radiation (SDLR) plays a key role in the surface energy budget and climate system, yet its estimation under cloudy conditions remains uncertain. Cloud-base temperature (CBT)-based parameterizations using total-column atmospheric radiation and emissivity (TARE-CBT), although more physically interpretable than data-driven models, often introduce systematic biases in kilometer-scale SDLR estimation due to oversimplified representations of atmospheric and cloud radiative contributions. To address this issue, this study develops a physically consistent CBT-based parameterization (SARE-CBT) that separates cloud-base emission and subcloud atmospheric contributions using a new formulation of subcloud emissivity dependent on the subcloud atmospheric profile. The proposed SARE-CBT parameterization is systematically evaluated against three conventional TARE-CBT parameterizations using radiative-transfer (RT) simulations, ground-based observations, and satellite retrievals based on MODIS and ERA5. Across all three evaluation datasets, SARE-CBT consistently outperforms TARE-CBT models, achieving root-mean-square error (RMSE) values of 7.0, 6.7–11.3, and 25.5 W/m2, respectively. The improvement is most pronounced under low-cloud and optically moderate-to-thick cloud conditions, reducing RMSE by 5.2–6.2 W/m2 and substantially mitigating the systematic overestimation of SDLR. Mechanism analysis indicates that using subcloud rather than total-column atmospheric emissivity enables a more accurate representation of atmospheric and cloud-base radiative contributions. Consequently, SARE-CBT captures their physical dependence on cloud-base height (CBH) and reduces systematic bias in SDLR estimation. In addition, SARE-CBT produces different seasonal patterns of longwave cloud radiative forcing (LWCRF) compared to TARE-CBT, with lower estimates and stronger correlations with CBH. These findings highlight the importance of explicitly representing subcloud atmospheric emissivity and provide a physically interpretable framework for improving cloudy SDLR retrievals.
author: Shanshan Yu, Xiaozhou Xin, Qinhuo Liu, Hailong Zhang, Li Li

title: DiffRSMT: A Diffusion-Driven Interactive Multitask Learning Model for Joint Remote Sensing Image Segmentation, Height Estimation, and Boundary Detection
content: Remote sensing (RS) multitask learning (MTL) aims to jointly perform several interpretation tasks within a unified framework. However, existing MTL methods often treat these tasks as individual problems, but overlook the importance of task interactions. In this article, we propose a novel diffusion-driven MTL framework, named DiffRSMT, for joint RS image segmentation, height estimation, and boundary detection. Unlike existing approaches that require separate diffusion processes for each task, DiffRSMT deploys a unified diffusion framework, which consists of two main components: a label-unified encoding (LuE) module and a task-interactive decoding module. Specifically, the LuE module aggregates the heterogeneous task labels into a unified latent representation, enabling the network to effectively capture task-interactive features. The task-interactive decoding module employs a time-conditioned attention mechanism during the denoising phase to enhance the interactions between tasks, which can improve the model’s MTL capability. In addition, a time-conditioned residual convolution module is introduced to further refine the denoising process. Extensive experiments on multiple RS datasets demonstrate that DiffRSMT provides better performance than several state-of-the-art MTL methods. The code is available at https://github.com/sycs-2024/DiffRSMT
author: Yu Shen, Shifan Wu, Lin Cao, Liang Xiao, David Camacho, Qian Du, Qiaolin Ye

title: AnyFusion: Train Once, Fuse Anywhere—Universal Unsupervised Hyperspectral–Multispectral Image Fusion via Wavelength-Aware Spectral Set Transformer
content: Fusing a low-resolution hyperspectral image (LrHSI) with a high-resolution multispectral image (HrMSI) is a practical route to high-resolution hyperspectral imagery (HrHSI), yet real deployment faces three obstacles: no HrHSI supervision exists for a new sensor; sensors differ arbitrarily in band count, wavelength layout, spectral response function (SRF), and resolution ratio; and existing unsupervised methods reoptimize from scratch for every scene, so nothing carries over between images and, with no reference available, an unstable run cannot even be detected. We propose AnyFusion, a universal unsupervised fusion framework that is trained once and then adapted, without any HrHSI supervision, to arbitrary sensor configurations. AnyFusion represents every band as a token conditioned on its physical center wavelength and processes the band set with a spectral set Transformer (SST) whose attention is guided by wavelength and SRF-overlap biases; a wavelength-query decoder synthesizes arbitrary output bands at arbitrary spatial scales. The unknown degradation is estimated per scene by jointly learning an implicit neural point spread function (PSF) and a wavelength-conditional SRF; the learned operators match the fusion accuracy of the ground-truth operators without requiring knowledge of the kernel or of the sampling geometry. On this band-agnostic architecture, a cross-sensor universal pretraining stage driven purely by consistency losses yields a single checkpoint that transfers to unseen sensors. On four benchmarks, AnyFusion attains the best mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) among all compared unsupervised methods on three datasets, consistent pretraining gains of +0.62 to +2.77 dB with 2.0– $3.3\times $  fewer adaptation iterations at matched from-scratch (FS) quality, and strong generalization across spatial scales, band subsets, wavelength ranges, and SRFs. On a real ZY1-02D spaceborne pair with no reference, a checkpoint pretrained solely on the simulated benchmarks raises spectral observation consistency by +5.18 dB (+2.79 dB when all runs are scored with the sensor-nominal SRF) while converging roughly an order of magnitude faster, supporting “train once, fuse anywhere.”
author: Ke Zheng, Qianqian Zhao, Lianru Gao, Haoyang Yu, Jiaxin Li, Bing Zhang

title: PHANTOM: Physics-Informed Hyperspectral Adversarial Network for Transformer-Optimized Methane Detection
content: Accurate detection of methane plumes in hyperspectral imagery is critical for environmental monitoring and greenhouse gas emission assessment. Traditional detection methods often struggle with complex atmospheric conditions, background variability, and subtle spectral signatures. We introduce the physics-informed hyperspectral adversarial network for transformer-optimized methane (PHANTOM) detection, a novel hybrid deep learning architecture that integrates physics-based constraints with advanced neural networks for robust methane plume segmentation. Our model’s core is a U-Net generator with an integrated Transformer bottleneck, designed to capture both local and global spatial dependencies in the data to produce high-fidelity methane abundance maps. The framework is uniquely constrained by two physical principles: 1) a Beer–Lambert reconstruction loss, which models the physical attenuation of surface radiance through the gas plume using a dedicated background estimation network and 2) a reaction–diffusion partial differential equation (PDE) loss, which regularizes the solution to encourage the spatial structure of the predicted plume to be physically plausible. An adversarial discriminator further refines the output, ensuring the generated maps are structurally indistinguishable from ground truth labels. By deeply integrating these physical priors into the training objective, our method produces results that are more physically consistent, robust, and interpretable than traditional data-driven approaches. Benchmarked against the state-of-the-art HyperSTARCOP model, PHANTOM demonstrates superior performance across all evaluation metrics with seven times fewer parameters. It also transfers to the independent spaceborne EMIT dataset without architectural changes, roughly doubling the  $F1$  score of matched filter (MF) baselines.
author: Sachin Giri, Derek Hollenbeck, Rafal Krzysiak, YangQuan Chen, Wan Du

title: DBRAMamba: A Gradually Refined Mamba Network Developed for Damaged Building Remote Sensing Assessment From Coarse to Fine After the Earthquake
content: Remote sensing-based assessment of earthquake-induced building damage using pre-event and postevent bitemporal imagery is essential for rapidly determining the spatial distribution and severity of damage after destructive earthquakes. However, reliable assessment remains challenging because cross-temporal imaging differences may generate pseudo-changes, damaged buildings often exhibit fragmented and ambiguous boundaries, and different damage levels are characterized by irregular and highly variable spatial morphologies. To address these challenges, we propose DBRAMamba, a disaster-oriented semantic change detection (SCD) framework that performs postearthquake building damage assessment (BDA) in a coarse-to-fine manner. A Siamese VMamba backbone is employed to extract hierarchical bitemporal representations. In the change decoder, a global–local contrastive module (GLCM) combines local temporal contrast with long-range structural context to enhance damage-related changes while suppressing irrelevant cross-temporal differences, and an edge-guided module (EGM) introduces structure-aware boundary information to refine damaged-building localization. In the semantic decoder, a deformable edge refinement module (DERM) adaptively models irregular damage morphology and refines structural boundaries for damage-level discrimination. Experiments on the Dingri earthquake-damaged building dataset show that DBRAMamba achieves  $\mathbf {F}_{\mathbf {1}}^{\mathbf {cd}}$ -,  $\mathbf {F}_{\mathbf {1}}^{\mathbf {clf}}$ -, and  $\mathbf {F}_{\mathbf {1}}^{\mathbf {o}}$ -scores of 73.99%, 68.80%, and 70.36%, respectively, obtaining the best damage-classification and overall performance among the evaluated SCD methods while maintaining competitive localization accuracy. Cross-scene experiments on the Jishishan earthquake dataset further demonstrate robust transfer performance, where DBRAMamba achieves the highest  $\mathbf {F}_{\mathbf {1}}^{\mathbf {cd}}$ , Kappa, and  $\mathbf {F}_{\mathbf {1}}^{\mathbf {o}}$ . Under the conventional xBD BDA setting, the adapted DBRAMamba (BDA) also achieves the highest  $\mathbf {F}_{\mathbf {1}}^{\mathbf {clf}}$  and  $\mathbf {F}_{\mathbf {1}}^{\mathbf {o}}$  among the evaluated convolutional neural network (CNN)-, Transformer-, and Mamba-based approaches. Additional analyses of low-damage regions, nonseismic changes, and regional damage statistics further demonstrate the potential of DBRAMamba for rapid postearthquake-damaged-building mapping and disaster-response-oriented assessment.
author: Yuanhao Wang, Shumin Wang, Ziying Gu, Kunyang Yang, Yitong Wang, Kangsan Yu, Aixia Dou, Zongxu Pan, Wei Ke, Xiangkun Kong, Xuehua Zhang, Duo A

title: Physically Induced Atmospheric Adversarial Perturbations: Enhancing Transferability and Robustness in Remote Sensing Image Classification
content: Adversarial attacks pose a severe threat to the reliability of deep learning models in remote sensing (RS) image classification. Most existing methods rely on direct pixelwise perturbations, failing to exploit the inherent atmospheric characteristics of RS imagery or survive real-world image degradations. In this article, we propose FogFool, an atmospherically inspired digital-domain adversarial framework that generates visually plausible fog-based perturbations by iteratively optimizing Perlin noise-initialized atmospheric patterns. By modeling fog formations with natural, irregular structures, FogFool generates adversarial examples that are not only visually consistent with authentic RS scenes but also deceptive. By leveraging the spatial coherence and mid-to-low-frequency nature of atmospheric phenomena, FogFool embeds adversarial information into structural features shared across diverse architectures. Extensive experiments on two benchmark RS datasets demonstrate that FogFool achieves superior performance: not only does it exceed in white-box settings but also exhibits exceptional black-box transferability reaching 83.74% transfer attack success rates (TASRs) and robustness against common preprocessing-based defenses such as JPEG compression (JC) and filtering. Detailed analyses, including confusion matrices and class activation map (CAM) visualizations, reveal that our atmospheric-driven perturbations induce a universal shift in model attention. These results indicate that FogFool represents a practical, stealthy, and highly persistent threat to RS classification systems, providing a robust benchmark for evaluating model reliability in complex environments.
author: Weiwei Zhuang, Wangze Xie, Qi Zhang, Xia Du, Zihan Lin, Zheng Lin, Hanlin Cai, Jizhe Zhou, Zihan Fang, Chi-Man Pun, Wei Ni, Jun Luo

title: Assessing the Impacts of Land use Optimization under Multiple Scenarios on Carbon Storage for Advancing SDG Reporting: Implications Derived From an Integrated Simulation Framework
content: Predicting the impacts of prospective land use on carbon storage (CS) under different development strategies provides crucial knowledge for achieving sustainable development goals (SDGs). However, conventional cellular automata (CA) models often overlook mixed structures and competition within land units, and how multi-scenario land use optimization integrating quantitative composition and spatial allocation affects CS and SDGs remains unclear. We developed an ensemble framework coupling autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA)-multi-objective programming (MOP), mixed-cell cellular automata (MCCA) and integrated valuation of ecosystem services and trade-offs (InVEST) models to explore CS responses to optimized land use under four scenarios in Guanzhong Plain urban agglomeration by 2040, quantify land use change contributions to CS via a carbon storage change index, and assess effects on SDG15.1.1 (Proportion of forest area) and SDG15.3.1 (Proportion of degraded land). During 2000-2020, cropland and grassland declined substantially while built-up areas expanded rapidly. By 2040, projections demonstrated the highest CS gain under the ecological protection scenario (EPS) and the greatest loss under the economic development scenario (EDS). The heterogeneity of CS was governed by carbon sink regions, ecological spaces, and carbon density. Forest conservation notably benefited CS, whereas urban sprawl had pronounced negative impacts. Interaction detection revealed bivariate or nonlinear enhancement effects. EPS most effectively promoted SDG15.1.1 but yielded the lowest SDG15.3.1; EDS contributed least to SDG15.1.1. Improving CS and SDG15.1.1 forest coverage alone insufficiently reversed SDG15.3.1 land degradation trends. Interannual CS uncertainty exceeded inter-scenario uncertainty. These findings inform targeted land use planning, carbon neutrality strategies, and SDG advancement.
author: Tingting Zou, Ping Zhang, Jiexuan Liu, Huanyuan Wang, Yue Huang, Lina Sun, Jinbao Liu, Ying Pan, Wenping Liu, Xiang Li, Kang Hou, Yucheng Zhu, Yu Huang

title: Frozen Vision–Language Priors and Multilook Supervision for Diffusion-Based SAR Image Despeckling
content: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery is corrupted by signal-dependent multiplicative speckle. Because clean references are generally unavailable for real acquisitions, many supervised despeckling networks rely on synthetic clean–noisy pairs and must generalize across sensors with different look counts. Existing diffusion-based despecklers model speckle statistics with increasing fidelity, yet often leave the semantic context of the underlying scene—which governs which edges and textures must be preserved—untapped. We show that a single forward pass of an off-the-shelf vision–language image encoder, applied directly to the noisy SAR input, supplies a scene-level prior strong enough to guide a diffusion despeckler. We propose a clean-target denoising diffusion implicit model whose denoising network receives a frozen vision–language image embedding through adaptive layer normalization at every block, supervised on a multilook fully developed-speckle pool. On the held-out mixed-look synthetic validation set, the model attains 33.85-dB peak signal-to-noise ratio, 0.907 structural similarity, and an edge-preservation index of 0.840. A separately trained source-disjoint audit replicate obtains 33.92-dB peak signal-to-noise ratio and 0.908 structural similarity on its independent test split. A single checkpoint generalizes to two real-world distributions without retraining, attaining edge-preservation indices of 0.889 on a public benchmark of paired noisy and prefiltered intensity-domain SAR images and 0.971 on a held-out spaceborne C-band ground-range-detected set.
author: Haoquan Zhai, Hongjun Song

title: Vision–Language Multimodal State Space Network for UAV-Based Soil Moisture Change Detection
content: With the increasing application of uncrewed aerial vehicle remote sensing technology in precision agriculture, the detection of changes in soil moisture content using high-resolution imagery faces challenges, such as irregular patch shapes, a lack of semantic information, and difficulties in modeling long-range dependencies. To address these challenges, this article proposes a vision–language multimodal state space network (VLM-SSNet). This method constructs a multiscale deformation-aware feature fusion module to accurately capture irregular soil boundaries and multiscale textures; introduces a vision–language cross-modal interaction module to reduce visual ambiguity using semantic priors; and designs a multipath fusion state space module to achieve efficient global long-range modeling with linear computational complexity. Experimental results demonstrate that VLM-SSNet performs exceptionally well in detecting changes in soil moisture content, achieving an $F_{1}$-score of 90.92% and an mIoU of 80.14%, representing significant improvements over mainstream methods. Furthermore, the model exhibits excellent generalization capabilities under complex resolution conditions and in the presence of noise interference, providing reliable technical support for the precise monitoring of farmland.
author: Ke Wu, Yang Li, Kai Fang, Sezai Ercisli

title: Validation Framework and Quality Assessment of the OPERA Sentinel-1 Radiometric Terrain Correction (RTC-S1) Product
content: As synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data become increasingly central to global Earth observation, the observational products for end-users from remote sensing analysis (OPERA) project has released a near-global radiometric terrain correction (RTC) product derived from Sentinel-1 (RTC-S1). This fully calibrated and geocoded dataset forms the basis for higher-level OPERA products, such as dynamic surface water extent (DSWx-S1) and Disturbance (DIST-S1), while making SAR data accessible to a broader range of nonexpert users. Despite the documented value of RTC data, the lack of standardized evaluation protocols has presented a challenge for product assurance. This article addresses this gap by proposing a comprehensive, reusable framework designed to standardize the assessment of geometric and radiometric accuracy for RTC products. We summarize the processing concepts and project requirements behind OPERA RTC-S1, then apply our proposed framework to RTC-S1 data across a suite of global validation sites. Results demonstrate that OPERA RTC-S1 consistently meets or exceeds defined product requirements, establishing it as a high-quality data baseline for downstream applications. Applying the proposed validation framework to OPERA data confirms its utility as a reusable, standardized template for evaluating RTC products from various providers or sensors.
author: Franz J Meyer, Alexander Lewandowski, Gustavo H. X. Shiroma, Seongsu Jeong, Heresh Fattahi

title: Understanding Phase Difference PolSAR Data From an Extended Cardioid Distribution
content: Modeling angular data from phase difference polarimetric synthetic aperture radar (PDPolSAR) is essential for accurately describing phase-related quantities that contain relevant geophysical information. The Cardioid (C) distribution is a classical and widely used model for circular data; however, it does not capture the asymmetry and multimodality often observed in real PolSAR phase differences. To address this limitation, we propose an extended C law, called the exponentiated Cardioid (EC) distribution. We derive some of its main properties, including trigonometric moments, skewness, and kurtosis. Two estimation methods for the EC parameters are considered: maximum likelihood and quantile least squares, and their performance is evaluated through Monte Carlo experiments. We then apply the proposed model as a statistical descriptor of PDPolSAR using E-SAR data. The results indicate that the EC model provides a competitive and often improved fit compared to classical circular distributions, namely, the C and von Mises distributions, as well as the physically derived multilook phase difference distribution. These findings highlight its potential to enhance the statistical modeling of angular features in remote sensing applications.
author: Fernanda V. Paula, Getúlio J. A. Amaral, Abraão D. C. Nascimento

title: Gap Filling in Satellite Time Series: In Search of Simple Yet Reliable Reconstruction Methods
content: Complete and temporally consistent satellite image time series are essential for many Earth observation applications. This study formulates gap filling as a postmask reconstruction problem and introduces two transparent operators that require neither external supervised training nor area-specific fine-tuning. Hypercomplex bases (HCB) reconstruct missing observations directly from the spectro-temporal structure of the observed time series, whereas a knowledge-based approach named HELIX additionally exploits land-cover information through analytically estimated class-specific seasonal guidance. Reconstruction fidelity is first examined under spatially heterogeneous clustered cloud/shadow missingness, where unaffected observations from the same acquisition remain available. HCB and HELIX retain low spectral-angle deviations of 7.9$^\circ$ and 8.2$^\circ$, respectively, together with comparatively limited spatial-gradient and temporal-gradient changes and without the pronounced structural artifacts observed for several learned baselines. To isolate temporal reconstruction under common support conditions, a complementary complete-date benchmark removes entire acquisitions and systematically varies temporal support across seven study areas, all five main Köppen–Geiger climate groups, two years, 30 controlled gap scenarios, four spectral bands, and 11 land-cover classes. In this benchmark, HELIX achieves the lowest aggregate mean absolute error (MAE 688.4 DN), median absolute error (MedAE 188 DN), root-mean-square error (RMSE 1636.4 DN), and mean spectral angle mapper (SAM 7.38$^\circ$), while HCB follows with an MAE of 879.4 DN, MedAE of 262 DN, RMSE of 1782.4 DN, and mean SAM of 7.88$^\circ$. Both remain stable under interpolation-like and extrapolation-like configurations with one-sided temporal support. HCB provides strong reconstruction and spectral fidelity at low computational cost without ancillary semantic information, whereas HELIX complements it through semantic seasonal constraints that improve radiometric accuracy. The two approaches therefore represent complementary transparent operating points for robust and auditable reconstruction of masked optical satellite time series.
author: Andreas Schmitt, Sarah Hauser

title: PFR-Det: Progressive Feature Refinement Small Object Detection Framework for UAV Images
content: Vision-based uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) detection, which encompasses both UAV-perspective observation and anti-UAV surveillance, is crucial for remote sensing, yet challenging due to resource constraints and complex environments. Targets are often tiny and submerged in background clutter, degrading detection accuracy. To bridge this gap, this article proposes a Progressive Feature Refinement small object detection framework (PFR-Det) based on YOLOv12. Specifically, a Pyramid Context C2f module extracts features from different receptive fields through parallel paths to enhance weak target representations. Furthermore, DySample is employed for dynamic upsampling in the neck to reconstruct fine-grained morphological details with high fidelity. In addition, an asymmetric spatial-channel attention module accentuates salient features while attenuating background noise, complemented by a lightweight GhostHead to streamline feature decoding. Comprehensive evaluations across VisDrone2019-DET, UAVDT, and DUT-AntiUAV benchmarks substantiate that PFR-Det strikes a superior balance between precision and latency. Notably, on VisDrone2019-DET, our model achieves an $mAP_{50}$ of 34.6%, surpassing the YOLOv12 baseline by 6.0% with merely 2.04 M parameters.
author: Bingbing Wei, Qingchuan Zhai, Xinying Zhang, Yuanke Zhang

title: Spatiotemporal Prediction of Grassland NDVI Dynamics Under Reduced Observation Support via Reliability-Aware Attention
content: Annual optical composites used for grassland vegetation forecasting contain spectral information supported by different numbers of observations retained after quality assessment (QA) screening. Spectral content and retained observation counts describe complementary aspects of these inputs, yet standard content-based attention does not explicitly use the latter when assigning feature contributions. In this article, we introduce reliability-aware attention (RA-Attn) to condition the use of spectral histories on their observation support. Relative QA-retained counts regulate feature selection and propagation, allowing the model to account for acquisition support while preserving content-dependent interactions and adding no trainable parameters. Using annual Landsat inputs from 2013 to 2024, we forecast annual changes in the normalized difference vegetation index ($\Delta$NDVI) for 2025 across three geographic site-holdout folds covering 12 Chinese grassland sites. RA-Attn achieves an overall root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.0606, compared with 0.0725 for SimVP and 0.0720 for pixelwise historical climatology. It also yields the lowest mean RMSE and mean absolute error among the evaluated methods in every natural QA-rejection and cloud-burden stratum. The gains over both learned models and historical climatology support the predictive value of conditioning feature use on acquisition support. QA-retained observation records can, therefore, guide how spectral histories are used after compositing, linking each pixel's observational basis to grassland forecasting.
author: Zihuan Wang, Chenyu Zhou, Fangyu He, Jianxi Huang, Tianyi Wang

title: FL-MHSM: Spatially Adaptive Fusion and Ensemble Learning for Flood–Landslide Multihazard Susceptibility Mapping at Regional Scale
content: Existing multihazard susceptibility mapping (MHSM) studies often rely on spatially uniform models, treat hazards independently, and provide limited representation of interhazard dependence and predictive uncertainty. To address these limitations, this study proposes FL-MHSM, a spatially adaptive framework for regional flood–landslide susceptibility mapping that combines two-level spatial partitioning, probabilistic early fusion (EF), hazard-specific late fusion (LF), and an uncertainty-aware soft-gating mixture of experts (MoE), with MoE serving as the final predictive model. The spatial organization distinguishes data-parallel grids from contextual zoning for localized modeling, while a controlled experiment shows that the benefit of contextual partitioning increases when the underlying hazard–factor relationships are spatially heterogeneous rather than arising from subdivision alone. In Kerala, EF remained competitive with LF, improving flood recall from 0.816 to 0.840 and reducing the Brier score from 0.092 to 0.086, while MoE provided the strongest performance for flood susceptibility, achieving an area under the curve (AUC)–receiver operating characteristic (ROC) of 0.905, recall of 0.930, and F1-score of 0.722. In Nepal, EF similarly improved flood recall from 0.820 to 0.858 and reduced the Brier score from 0.057 to 0.049 relative to LF, while MoE outperformed both EF and LF for landslide susceptibility, achieving an AUC–ROC of 0.914, recall of 0.901, and F1-score of 0.559. The learned MoE contributions varied across hazards and contextual zones, indicating the need for adaptive models rather than fixed LF–EF integration. GeoDetector analysis of the MoE outputs further showed that dominant factors varied more across zones in Kerala, where susceptibility was shaped by different combinations of topographic, land-cover, and drainage-related controls, while Nepal showed a more consistent influence of topographic and glacier-related factors across zones. These findings show that EF and LF provide complementary predictive behavior, and that their spatially adaptive integration through MoE yields robust overall predictive performance for FL-MHSM while supporting interpretable characterization of multihazard susceptibility in spatially heterogeneous landscapes.
author: Aswathi Mundayatt, Jaya Sreevalsan-Nair

title: Automated Estimation of Stand-Level Merchantable Stem Volume in Temperate Forests Using Mobile Backpack LiDAR Systems
content: Stand-level merchantable stem volume estimation in temperate forests is critical for data-driven forest management decision-making. Mobile light detection and ranging (LiDAR) has greatly improved data-collection efficiency, yet automated individual stem volume modeling from large, complex mobile LiDAR point clouds remains limited. This study presents an automated framework to estimate stand-level merchantable stem volume from backpack mobile LiDAR data. First, a stand-scale point cloud is reconstructed from input LiDAR scans using a simultaneous trajectory enhancement and mapping approach. Next, individual trees are segmented using a multistage geometric procedure to generate per-tree point clouds across the stand. For each segmented tree, merchantable stem volume is estimated through 1) initial skeletonization and graph derivation, 2) merchantable stem modeling, and 3) scan-vs-model-based adjustment, together with derivation of a scan-coverage confidence score that quantifies the degree of point-cloud support for each reconstructed stem and provides an internal quality-control indicator. The proposed approach was evaluated using leaf-off temperate natural forest datasets collected in Indiana, United States, with an in-house backpack mobile LiDAR system. Tree-level validation against destructively measured reference volumes for sampled stems at two test sites showed that the proposed method achieved coefficients of determination (R²) of 0.97 and 0.92, compared with baseline quantitative structure model (QSM) methods TreeQSM (0.90 and 0.83) and AdQSM (0.85 and 0.83). In addition, comparisons with species-level allometric models showed close overall agreement; however, potential taxon-level differences warrant further evaluation using sufficient independent reference data. The proposed framework can support applications ranging from individual tree analysis to stand-scale forest inventory with minimal manual intervention under leaf-off conditions in temperate natural forests.
author: Sangyoon Park, Hazem Hanafy, Chunxi Zhao, Jinyuan Shao, Noah Scott Lyon, Ayman Habib, Songlin Fei

title: Robust KLD-Based Homogeneous Pixel Selection for Phase-Linked Distributed Scatterer InSAR
content: Statistically homogeneous pixels (SHPs) are critical for distributed-scatterer InSAR because they control the accuracy of coherence matrix estimation, phase linking, and subsequent deformation inversion. Existing SHP selection methods commonly face a trade-off between robustness and efficiency: Nonparameteric tests are robust but computationally demanding, whereas parameteric tests are efficient but can be unstable with small image stacks or transient high-intensity scatterers. This article proposes a robust Kullback–Leibler divergence (KLD)-based SHP selection method for distributed-scatterer InSAR. The method jointly uses intensity, interferometric phase, and local coherence information. A robust M-estimator suppresses outliers in temporal mean intensity, quadtree segmentation provides efficient local coherence estimation, and a pixelwise adaptive threshold replaces a fixed global threshold. Simulation experiments and Sentinel-1 acquisitions over Shanghai from 2023 to 2024 were used to compare the proposed method with state-of-the-art methods. Results show that the proposed method improves selection stability in small-sample scenarios, enhances EMI-optimized phase quality, increases a posteriori coherence by about 0.2 in airport runway and terminal areas, and yields 301 092 high-coherence measurement points, representing a 30.6%–63.2% increase over the benchmarks. The real-data experiment over Changxing Island also demonstrates a noticeable improvement in phase quality and enables the identification of a larger number of DS pixels. Runtime tests show efficiency comparable to classic parameteric approaches and much faster processing than nonparameteric tests. The method provides an efficient and robust SHP selection option for phase-linked multitemporal InSAR processing.
author: Xin Gao, Hongyu Liang, Lei Zhang, Bochen Zhang, Songbo Wu

title: SDSFormer: Rethinking Hyperspectral Change Detection via Adaptive Spectral Sampling
content: Hyperspectral change detection (HSI-CD) aims to identify land-cover changes from bitemporal hyperspectral imagery. However, the high spectral dimensionality and nonuniform distribution of discriminative information pose significant challenges for change representation learning. Existing Transformer-based HSI-CD methods typically perform uniform spectral aggregation across all bands, making them susceptible to spectral redundancy and irrelevant spectral variations. To address this issue, we rethink HSI-CD from the perspective of adaptive spectral sampling and propose a novel spectral deformable attention (SDA) mechanism. By extending deformable learning from the spatial domain to the spectral domain, SDA dynamically learns spectral offsets to focus on informative spectral regions while preserving long-range spectral dependencies. Based on SDA, we develop a spectral-aware Transformer framework, termed spectral deformable sampling transformer (SDSFormer), which integrates adaptive spectral representation learning and cross-temporal spectral alignment for discriminative change feature extraction. Extensive experiments on three public benchmark datasets, including Farmland, Santa Barbara, and Bay Area, demonstrate that SDSFormer consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits strong robustness and data efficiency, attaining superior detection accuracy with only 1% labeled training samples. These results validate the effectiveness of adaptive spectral sampling and highlight its potential as a promising paradigm for hyperspectral representation learning and change detection.
author: Qinsen Liu, Bangyong Sun, Zhiyong Lv, Pengchang Zhang, Xiangpeng Feng, Tao Yu, Bingliang Hu

title: PDQ-DETR: Parallel Multiscale Perception With Density-Guided Dynamic Query Detection Transformer for Small-Object Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery
content: Detection Transformer (DETR) and its variants have made significant progress in small-object detection in remote sensing through end-to-end set prediction and global context modeling. However, existing DETR-based methods struggle to simultaneously accommodate the distinct feature-modeling requirements of small objects in satellite and uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) imagery and the different query-allocation requirements of sparse, medium-density, and dense small-object scenes. Specifically, small objects in satellite imagery typically occupy only a few pixels and provide limited fine-grained cues, such as textures and edges. These cues are further attenuated by successive downsampling, making it difficult for deep features to preserve sufficient small-object details. Small objects in UAV imagery, by contrast, exhibit more pronounced scale variations. Moreover, the number and spatial density of small objects differ substantially among the three scene types in both forms of imagery. To address these challenges, we propose parallel multiscale perception with density-guided dynamic query detection Transformer (PDQ-DETR) for small-object detection in satellite and UAV imagery. First, a Parallel Multiscale Dual-Gated Feature Fusion module extracts features for small objects at different scales and selectively fuses shallow high-resolution features with deep features, thereby preserving small-object details while adapting to small-object scale variations. Second, a density-guided dynamic query mechanism uses density features and a location map to highlight potential small-object regions and suppress background responses. It dynamically adjusts the number of queries according to the number and spatial density of small objects in each image and guides initial query position selection. Finally, a density-adaptive gaussian map generation strategy provides a supervision signal with more compact responses in dense regions for location-map learning, reducing the interference of overlapping responses from adjacent small objects on initial query position selection. PDQ-DETR achieves $\text{mAP}$ values of 39.4%, 34.2%, and 47.9% on VisDrone, AI-TOD v2, and DOTA 2.0, respectively, ranking among the leading methods in comparisons with existing advanced approaches. These results validate its small-object detection performance in both satellite and UAV remote sensing scenarios.
author: Yeqiang Gao, Wenqing Feng, Wei Xu, Fangli Guan, Hu Yang, Fuping Liao, Tan Ke

title: Fire-Aware Cross-Modal Alignment and Modality–Adaptive Fusion Framework for UAV-Based RGB–Thermal Fire and Smoke Detection
content: Reliable fire and smoke detection using uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-borne RGB–thermal remote sensing imagery is important for early wildfire monitoring. In practical UAV-based RGB–thermal remote sensing systems, however, sensor misalignment, changing modality reliability, platform-induced viewpoint variations, and weak cues from small early-stage fire targets often reduce detection accuracy. This article presents a fire-aware cross-modal alignment and modality–adaptive fusion (FCAMF) framework for UAV-based RGB–thermal fire and smoke detection. FCAMF preferentially aligns infrared features to RGB references in fire-relevant regions through a fire-aware deformable alignment module, reducing cross-modal spatial inconsistency while limiting unnecessary background deformation. To strengthen the infrared branch, a lightweight fire feature extractor is used to enhance compact thermal responses and suppress background thermal noise. The aligned RGB and infrared features are then integrated by a modality-aware mixture-of-experts module, which adjusts modality contributions according to scene conditions. Experiments on the RGBT-3 M dataset show that FCAMF achieves 71.5% mAP$_{50\text{--}95}$, 96.4% mAP$_{50}$, and 94.7% precision, yielding better localization quality than single-modality and RGB–thermal baselines. Results on the RGB–Thermal Wildfire dataset also show good robustness under different imaging conditions. These results suggest that selective alignment and adaptive fusion are effective for UAV-based early wildfire detection.
author: Dianwei Wang, Kang Yang, Jie Fang, Yuanqing Li, Da Ai, Jiapeng Yan, Jianing Tang

title: SP-Mamba: Structure-Preserving State-Space Modeling for Hyperspectral Image Classification
content: Mamba has recently shown great potential for hyperspectral image (HSI) classification. However, existing Mamba-based methods often disrupt the intrinsic 3-D spectral–spatial structure during sequence construction by either embedding spectral information into channels or modeling spectral and spatial sequences separately. Such structural misalignment hinders the modeling of joint spectral–spatial dependencies and limits classification performance. To address this issue, we propose a structure-preserving Mamba (SP-Mamba) framework for HSI classification. At the core of SP-Mamba is a structure-preserving spectral–spatial sequence modeling (SP-SSM) mechanism that enables state-space models to operate on structure-consistent spectral–spatial sequences. Specifically, SP-SSM first organizes spectral information into a unified 3-D spectral–spatial representation through spectral tokenization. A structure-preserving 3-D spectral–spatial serialization strategy is then applied to transform the resulting 3-D representation into sequences while maintaining spectral continuity and spatial neighborhood relationships. State-space modeling is subsequently performed along these structure-consistent sequences to capture long-range spectral–spatial dependencies. Furthermore, we introduce a 3-D spectral–spatial positional encoding module to explicitly encode spectral–spatial positional information, which provides complementary positional cues to further enhance serialized spectral–spatial sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that SP-Mamba achieves strong and consistent performance against state-of-the-art methods, notably reaching 92.16% overall accuracy on the challenging HanChuan dataset and showing at least a 2.87% improvement. These results highlight the importance of explicitly preserving the 3-D spectral–spatial organization for effectively exploiting the potential of state-space models in HSI classification.
author: Runmin Lei, Yuchuan Zhou, Xiang Zhang, Huizhou Zhou, Xinpeng Zhang

title: Reliability-Enhanced State-Space Interaction for Robust Remote Sensing Change Detection
content: Remote sensing change detection aims to identify land-cover changes from bitemporal images acquired over the same area. Although existing deep learning methods have achieved promising performance, they still suffer from pseudochanges caused by illumination variation, seasonal difference, shadows, sensor inconsistency, and slight spatial misalignment. Moreover, most bitemporal interaction strategies propagate temporal discrepancies without explicitly judging their reliability, which may amplify appearance-induced perturbations as change cues. To address these issues, we propose a reliability-aware change-guided state-space interaction framework for robust remote sensing change detection. Specifically, we first use temporal-consistent feature preparation (TCFP) to produce temporally comparable and locally refined hierarchical features. Then, a reliability-enhanced change-guided interaction module is designed to estimate change-evidence reliability and appearance-perturbation uncertainty from complementary state-space discrepancy representations. These reliability measurements are further introduced into the selective state-space interaction to regulate state writing, reading, and updating during bitemporal feature propagation. Finally, a lightweight hierarchical decoder combines the fused change representations and TCFP-prepared temporal detail cues to generate the final change map. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving intersection over union/F1 scores of 90.61%/95.07%, 84.29%/91.48%, 90.39%/94.95%, 55.75%/71.59%, 91.67%/95.65%, and 53.50%/69.71% on BCDD, LEVIR-CD, GoogleBuilding, CLCD, DSIFN, and SECOND, respectively.
author: Anbin Yu

title: CFformer: A Spatial-Frequency Model for Low-Light Remote Sensing Image Enhancement
content: Low-light remote sensing (RS) images often cover large scenes with spatially continuous structures and ground objects at varying scales, making it difficult to recover scene-wide structures while preserving fine details under nonuniform illumination and noise. Closely related RS methods generally organize frequency modeling around predefined amplitude–illumination and phase–structure roles. In contrast, we propose Conv-Fourier-Metaformer (CFformer), a self-attention-free MetaFormer that adaptively coordinates local spatial cues and global frequency context at the feature level. To recover scene-wide structures while preserving local details, its SF-Mixer combines parallel spatial and frequency modeling with input-adaptive channel recalibration and frequency-position modulation. To represent ground objects at varying scales, MSG-FFN employs multiple receptive fields for scale-aware feature modulation. Because shallow encoder features retain useful details but may also contain noise-contaminated responses, AFM adaptively regulates their injection through skip connections to preserve details while limiting the transfer of noise-contaminated responses. Extensive experiments on multiple low-light RS datasets and general low-light benchmarks demonstrate that CFformer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods while better preserving structural consistency and fine-grained ground-object details.
author: Jun Zhang, Liangliang Zheng, Xiaobin Wu, Tan Gao, Xiaotian Bai, Mengke Zhang, Yuanfu Yuan, Shuhan Zhang

title: Width-Adaptive Topology-Aware Distillation for Lightweight Road Extraction in Remote Sensing
content: Road extraction from remote sensing imagery is essential for disaster emergency response and infrastructure monitoring. Lightweight segmentation models are well suited to large-area and high-frequency applications because of their low parameter counts and short inference latency. However, their limited representation capacity often causes discontinuities in structurally vulnerable regions, including narrow branches, intersections, and occluded road segments. Existing topology constraints and knowledge distillation methods can improve structural representation, but full-image supervision tends to dilute informative structural signals in these critical regions. To address this problem, we propose a width-adaptive topology-aware distillation (WATD) framework for lightweight remote sensing road extraction. WATD constructs width-adaptive structurally sensitive regions by adjusting skeleton and boundary bands according to local road width. Within these regions, it combines probability-level, feature-level, and structure-level distillation with soft-skeleton-based continuous centerline supervision to transfer semantic and topological knowledge from a teacher network to a lightweight student. We also construct the Xiong'an area rural road dataset (XARRD) from multiseason GaoFen-1 imagery to support cross-domain and cross-temporal evaluation. On DeepGlobe, WATD improves intersection over union (IoU) by 4.55 percentage points and increases the road-network connectivity metric (Conn) from 67.45% to 78.95% over the MobileNetV2Seg baseline, without increasing inference cost. It also outperforms full-image topology distillation and fixed-region distillation in connectivity. In DeepGlobe-to-XARRD transfer, WATD yields the smallest IoU drop of 6.00% among the compared methods. These results show that directing structural constraints to width-adaptive vulnerable regions improves road-network connectivity while preserving lightweight inference and remaining robust under the evaluated domain shift.
author: Ruihao Li, Yating Zhang, Zifan Zhang, Zixuan Xie, Sihao Li, Xiaomin Tian

title: SPGMamba-CD: Superpixel-Guided Remote Sensing Building Change Detection With Mamba Network
content: Building change detection (BCD) enables precise localization of buildings and identification of changed building areas, supporting applications, such as illegal construction monitoring, disaster emergency response, and smart city management. Currently, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers are widely adopted for BCD. However, CNNs are limited by local receptive fields, whereas transformers suffer from quadratic complexity as image resolution increases. Moreover, existing methods struggle to effectively capture local information in multiscale building change regions due to fixed convolutional kernel sizes. In this article, a superpixel-guided Mamba-based method for BCD (SPGMamba-CD) is proposed to overcome the aforementioned challenges of multiscale representation and local modeling in high-resolution imagery. First, the SPGMamba-CD encoder employs a four-stage architecture to characterize multiscale building change information. Second, a superpixel-guided VSSBlock is designed as the fundamental module to adaptively extract both global and local features. It leverages superpixel spatial priors and a hierarchical superpixel scanning strategy to maintain spatial-semantic continuity, while dynamically aligning discriminative pixels with Mamba memory states. Furthermore, a bitemporal adaptive boundary geometry guidance module is introduced in the decoder to alleviate shadow-induced boundary ambiguity and enhance boundary representation. Experimental results on five public benchmark datasets, including GZ-CD, LEVIR-CD, LEVIR+-CD, WHU-CD, and uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-CD+, demonstrate that SPGMamba-CD achieves F1 scores of 88.66%, 91.08%, 84.01%, 91.23%, and 80.59%, and intersection over union scores of 79.64%, 83.63%, 72.42%, 83.88%, and 67.50%, respectively, consistently outperforming the compared methods. The SPGMamba-CD effectively reduces omission errors caused by multiscale buildings while producing more accurate and complete building boundaries under shadows and occlusions.
author: Rong Gui, Lihuan Tan, Zhaopu Song, Lei Wang, Huajian Zheng, Xinyan Li

title: TriFusion: A Unified CNN-Transformer Framework for Multiscale and Spectral-Spatial Learning in Hyperspectral Image Classification
content: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification remains challenging due to two fundamental issues: first, severe spectral redundancy and mixed spectral–spatial noise that degrade discriminability, and second, the difficulty of simultaneously capturing fine-grained local patterns and long-range contextual dependencies under limited labeled data.Existing convolutional neural network (CNN)-based methods excel at local feature extraction but fail to model global interactions, while Transformer-based models provide strong global modeling but are data-hungry and often overlook local spectral–spatial cues. To address these problems, we propose TriFusion, a unified CNN–Transformer hybrid framework that systematically integrates multiscale and spectral–spatial learning within a coherent fusion architecture. Specifically, an efficient spectral–spatial convolutional block is introduced to disentangle and enhance local spectral–spatial features while suppressing redundancy. A multiscale context module is further employed to aggregate contextual information. In addition, a deep feature pyramid progressively fuses hierarchical representations to preserve discriminative spectral–spatial semantics across scales. A lightweight Transformer encoder is finally incorporated to capture long-range dependencies. Extensive experiments on four widely used benchmarks (Pavia University, Salinas, WHU-Hi-Longkou, and Xuzhou) demonstrate that the proposed TriFusion framework consistently achieves the best overall accuracy among recent CNN-based, Transformer-based, and hybrid methods, with gains of 0.26–1.42 percentage points over the strongest competing baseline across the four datasets. Ablation studies and efficiency analyses further validate the effectiveness of each fusion component and the practical efficiency of the proposed design.
author: Feilong Fan, Anming Dong, En Li, Yanhui Guo

title: Terrain-Aware Fusion and Connectivity-Aware Learning Network for Great Wall Relic Extraction From Remote Sensing Imagery and Terrain Data
content: Great Wall relic extraction from high-resolution remote sensing (RS) imagery is important for cultural heritage discovery, mapping, and monitoring. However, this task remains challenging because mountainous relics often appear as narrow linear structures with weak visual contrast and are easily affected by vegetation cover, terrain shadows, and complex backgrounds. To address these challenges, this article proposes terrain-aware fusion and connectivity-aware learning network (TFCL-Net) for mountainous Great Wall relic extraction using optical RS imagery and terrain priors. Specifically, the terrain-aware fusion module integrates digital elevation model (DEM) and ridge information at different network depths, allowing the model to better exploit terrain priors for relic localization and representation. The connectivity-aware learning module improves the continuity of narrow wall predictions and reduces local discontinuities. In addition, a structure-conditioned image synthesis strategy generates synthetic images with clearer relic traces, and an adaptive filtering step removes unreliable samples. To support model training and evaluation, we construct a multisource Beijing Great Wall relic dataset that includes high-resolution optical RS imagery, DEM data, ridge prior maps, and polygon-level ground truth annotations. A three-level evaluation system, including pixel-level, centerline-level, and relaxed-level metrics, is adopted to assess both segmentation accuracy and structural quality. Experimental results across repeated runs show that TFCL-Net achieves 73.33% IoU and 84.61% F1-score, as well as 94.13% centerline quality and 89.42% relaxed IoU. These results indicate that the proposed framework can support Great Wall relic discovery, mapping, and monitoring in mountainous environments.
author: Daoyuan Zheng, Zhaohui Guo, Tiancheng Liu, Haixia Feng, Jiazheng Jiang, Mingyao Ai, Pengcheng Zhao, Shaohua Wang, Zhipeng Chen, Qingwu Hu

title: Spectral–Spatial Collaborative Calibration for Multisource Domain-Adaptive Semantic Segmentation of Remote Sensing Images
content: Multisource unsupervised domain adaptation (MS-UDA) can reduce the annotation burden of remote sensing semantic segmentation, but heterogeneous source spectra and ground sampling distances can destabilize target pseudolabels. This article presents a spectral–spatial collaborative calibration network (SSCCNet) for MS-UDA with RGB and infrared–red–green (IRRG) imagery. First, spectral adaptive normalization (SANM) performs category-conditioned statistical matching from the near-infrared channel of a labeled nonreference source to the red-channel statistics of an RGB reference source, while weak blending preserves source-specific contrast. Second, spatial granularity alignment filtering (SAF) provides resolution-aware contextual compensation for the lower-resolution Vaihingen branch through gated fusion of identity and dilated-convolution responses. Third, dual-threshold filtering (DTF) constructs detached pseudolabels from the current network, combining posterior-confidence screening with a restricted set of near-infrared intensity checks and class-aware weights. Experiments are conducted on two adaptation tasks constructed from ISPRS Potsdam RGB, Potsdam IRRG, and Vaihingen IRRG data. SSCCNet obtains mIoU/OA scores of 40.53%/64.00% and 57.82%/79.36% on the two tasks, respectively. In the cumulative ablation, performance increases at each stage as SANM, SAF, and DTF are introduced in sequence.

title: Latent Cluster Separation as a Regularizer for Lifelong Anomaly Detection
content:
arXiv:2611.03652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lifelong (continual) anomaly detection systems must learn a sequence of tasks without forgetting how to recognize anomaly types seen earlier -- a property known as backward transfer. A common way to try to improve backward transfer is to reshape a model's internal representation around learnable concept centroids, typically coupled with a new way of scoring anomalies based on distance to those centroids. Because these two design choices are usually introduced together, it is unclear which one is actually responsible for any performance gain. In this paper, we unbundle the two mechanisms within a VAE-based lifelong anomaly detector and study them separately. We find that used purely as a training-time regularizer -- while leaving anomaly scoring unchanged -- latent cluster separation can improve detection quality and backward transfer, though whether it outperforms the alternative scoring approach depends on the dataset's underlying representation. Switching to distance-based scoring is instead where most of the instability commonly associated with this class of method actually originates; we identify and explain the underlying mechanism. This benefit depends on the dataset's underlying representation, and we report this as practical guidance for choosing between the two design choices, rather than as a list of caveats.
author: Sabarish Radhakrishnan, Nathalie Japkowicz

title: Four Extensions of the Universal Law of Robustness: Log-Concave Covariates, Heterogeneous Mixtures, Vector-Valued Predictors, and Markovian Data
content:
arXiv:2611.03653v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Bubeck and Sellke's universal law of robustness says that fitting $n$ noisy samples below the noise level with a class of $p$ real parameters forces a Lipschitz constant of order $\sqrt{nd/p}$, when the covariate distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is isoperimetric: smooth interpolation costs a factor $d$ of overparametrization. Its hypotheses are Gaussian-type concentration, a homogeneous covariate law, scalar outputs, and independent samples; we relax each one. Exponential concentration suffices, at the unchanged rate and absolute constant and at the price of a capacity burn-in, some form of which we show is necessary; this gives the law for normalized log-concave covariates, with a $\log d$ loss from the current KLS bound. For heterogeneous mixtures the worst component constant is replaced by the weighted average of the component constants, under a typicality condition on the mixture composition. For vector-valued predictors the bound at the Frobenius Lipschitz scale is free of the output dimension $K$, and the Euclidean bound loses only $K^{-1/2}$, a loss that covariate-independent noise removes. Stationary Markov covariates retain the i.i.d. rate, the pseudo-spectral gap entering only the sample-size conditions. One master theorem carries the shared argument, and constants are explicit throughout.
author: Tobias J. Peter (ZHAW Zurich University of Applied Sciences)

title: Towards Automatic Heart Murmur Characterization from Multi-spot Phonocardiograms
content:
arXiv:2611.03654v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cardiac auscultation traditionally detects the presence of a heart murmur, but clinicians further characterize it by timing, shape, pitch, quality, and grade. Most automatic phonocardiogram analysis systems stop at binary detection and do not estimate this richer description. In this work, we formulate automatic murmur characterization as five patient-level classification tasks and compare three multi-spot strategies on recordings from the aortic, pulmonary, mitral, and tricuspid auscultation locations. First, classical and deep-learning classifiers are trained independently at each location, and predictions are combined via a maximum-severity late-fusion rule. Second, a synchronous multi-input CNN jointly processes one representative segment per location for a single task. Third, a unified multi-input, multi-output CNN predicts all five attributes from one shared multi-spot representation. Using 735 patients from the CirCor DigiScope dataset with complete four-spot recordings, the best late-fusion configurations reach an unweighted mean sensitivity between 85.56% and 93.81% across the five tasks, with class-specific recalls between 80.00% and 100.00% for every relevant category. The multi-input CNN trails late fusion by 7-16 points depending on the task, while the multi-output model reaches values between 72.59% and 79.40%, estimating all five attributes from one shared representation. We further show that naively balancing training data by adding all minority-class segments degrades patient-level performance under the maximum-severity rule, since it introduces non-representative, noisy segments not filtered by the clustering-based segment selection used for evaluation. These results indicate multi-spot murmur characterization is feasible with both fusion-based and jointly learned architectures, outlining a path toward automatic, structured murmur reports complementing binary screening.
author: Marcelo Nogueira, Jorge H. Oliveira, Carlos G. Ferreira, Miguel T. Coimbra, Al\'ipio M. Jorge

title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
content:
arXiv:2611.03655v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models often spread a concept across many internal dimensions, making their features difficult to interpret. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover clearer features after training. We ask whether models can instead learn interpretable output coordinates directly. We introduce Mixture of Wide Experts (MoWE), a sparse feed-forward layer in which selected experts read the full representation but write to fixed, disjoint output coordinates. On a controlled task with known hidden causes, this design preserves predictive performance while localizing causes more clearly than dense and standard mixture-of-experts (MoE) models.
  At approximately matched compute, we train two 19-layer runs of each architecture for 10 billion tokens. MoWE achieves evaluation cross-entropy 2.417 versus 2.452 for dense, while standard MoE reaches 2.22.
  We measure native-coordinate readability by asking a language-model judge to describe each coordinate from passages where it is strongly active and test that description on new passages. Correcting for descriptions that also fit other coordinates gives a specificity score of 0.523 for MoWE, 0.375 for dense, and 0.268 for standard MoE. TopK SAEs trained on the same FFN updates score 0.489 for dense and 0.556 for MoWE, making native MoWE comparable to the dense SAE.
  In the first case study, we identify a four-coordinate causal path supporting the model's prediction of degrees after the prompt A right angle is 90. We then copy seven angle-related coordinate values into the model as it processes A rectangle has four, changing its next-token prediction from sides to degrees. In the second, one fixed coordinate set detects hazardous requests and another steers the next token toward refusal. These examples show that MoWE combines sparse conditional computation with coordinates that can be identified and reused directly.
author: Tavish Mankash, Vardhaman Kalloli, Keshava Prasad, Deepan Muthirayan

title: Stress-Testing the Robustness of LLM-Based Causal Inference
content:
arXiv:2611.03656v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Why do some of the world's most powerful Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems still struggle to reason about cause and effect? Causal discovery, the ability to discern the underlying drivers of a system, is fundamental to scientific inquiry and has traditionally relied on structured data and statistical methods. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored as an alternative paradigm for causal inference, leveraging their broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite their linguistic fluency, LLMs often rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than genuine causal logic. While it is known that LLMs stumble in this domain, we lack a precise map of where, why, and how significantly these failures occur. In this paper, we propose a systematic stress-test framework across six critical dimensions: model scale, causal graph complexity, prompting strategy, metadata quality, data quality, and sensitivity to uncertainty. Our findings reveal a significant "optimism bias" in LLMs; models consistently overestimate causal links, leading to low precision across the board. Furthermore, we demonstrate that traditional evaluation metrics can be deceptive: while reasoning-heavy models lead in performance, the highest scores often occur when uncertainty in inference is overlooked. Once uncertainty is integrated into the evaluation, performance drops, providing a more honest reflection of causal reliability. We also find that, while scaling model size improves outcomes, these gains are fragile; performance degrades sharply as the quality of metadata decreases. This work serves as a practical guide to the blind spots of LLMs, offering a clear-eyed assessment of when these tools can be integrated into a causal discovery pipeline and when they are likely to lead researchers astray.
author: Ankitkumar Patel, Jigarkumar Patel, Amit Kumar, Supreetha Sreeram, Venkatesh Kulkarni

title: Learning Directional Randers Geometry for Latent-Space Exploration
content:
arXiv:2611.03675v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deep neural networks extract powerful latent representations from images, enabling fast and efficient downstream analysis. However, these latent spaces lack explicit geometric structure, leading to possibly poor interpolation fidelity and misleading extrapolation. Latent interpolation techniques assume symmetric transition costs which are often not the case for real world data. Their symmetric nature cannot capture directional processes, such as disease progression, where certain transitions are impossible (e.g. tumor growth dynamics or cognitive improvement in Alzheimer's disease). Although Riemannian metrics extend Euclidean geometry by incorporating curvature, they remain symmetric. We show that understanding asymmetry and not curvature alone directly addresses these problems. To do so we propose a new Finsler-Randers metric learning framework. It incorporates direction-dependent distances, thus enabling the computation of trajectories respecting monotonic sequential constraints. We demonstrate its potential for interpolation and extrapolation on controlled cross-sectional datasets.
author: Th\'eau Blanchard (HeKA | U1346, GE Healthcare), St\'ephanie Allassonni\`ere (CMAP)

title: Does the Trust Boundary Hold over Time? A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Receiver-Directed Federated Learning
content:
arXiv:2611.03724v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In receiver-directed federated learning, each site draws a trust boundary. For every source and model component it judges, on its own data, whether the transfer helps (admit), harms (reject) or cannot yet be told (abstain). We ask whether this boundary holds over hundreds of rounds. Our benchmark has a federation of thirteen semi-synthetic sites, an exact oracle for every evaluated transfer, paired seeds, an attack protocol, fourteen methods over 600 rounds and Qwen3-1.7B LoRA sites over 500. The answer depends on which boundary is measured. Across 20 paired CPU seeds, a gate judging against a fixed reference better identified transfers useful relative to the site's starting model. Yet it admitted 29% of transfers harmful to the model the site now has. A gate judging against the current model admitted 2% of harmful transfers on that target in the CPU tier, but missed many transfers useful to the starting model. Two short propositions explain these distinct failures. We also evaluate a held out audit that leaves gate verdicts intact. After training, it decides whether each final model is deployed or the site falls back to local training, and reports admissions that have gone stale. With independent audit data its guarantees hold after any training history. At 600 rounds the audit deployed 65 to 72% of models, none with negative benefit on its target, and kept 98% of the gain. No stale report had the wrong sign in our runs. With 20,000 audit observations, a variance-adaptive bound found 99% of stale transfers that cost at least 0.01 in log loss. A common-target Qwen3 comparison on 60 selected transfers shows the same tension over 100 rounds. With 38% adversarial sites, FedFomo and CS-Gate were the only evaluated methods with positive mean gain in every honest group.
author: Ting Xu, Henry Leung

title: Auditing a Model-Hub Benchmark: Data Quality, Training Budgets, and Side Information in HuggingBench
content:
arXiv:2611.03727v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Benchmarks built from model hubs combine interaction data, knowledge graphs (KGs) and resource documentation, but valid files do not ensure that these artifacts describe the same objects. Treating the release as a data product, we audit HuggingBench (SIGIR 2025), a benchmark for recommending Hugging Face resources, through data validation, a replication of its eleven recommendation methods and controlled experiments with three training seeds. In three of its four external KGs, the files pass key and range checks but violate the item-entity identity constraint on which KG recommenders rely. Correcting this join improves every KG-based method in every seed, by up to 73% in mean Recall@10, and consistently reverses ten of 27 comparisons between KG configurations. The protocol matters as well: the 100-epoch budget ends before early stopping in seven to eight of 29 validation-selected settings, and 21 of 23 such setting-seed pairs improve with a longer budget. The released item text, which no reported method uses, is the strongest signal: closed-form linear models with text and the item graph exceed the best reported Recall@10 by 18% while fitting in minutes on a CPU. Checks of other recommendation releases show that individually valid releases of one dataset can use incompatible identifiers. We release corrected files, mappings, validators and logs, and derive practices for preserving identity and provenance across the artifacts of benchmarks and model lakes.
author: Michal Podstawski

title: Minimal Superior Penalties: Characterising and Calibrating Decision-Aware Proper Scoring Rules
content:
arXiv:2611.03734v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training a classifier means letting a validation metric decide which model is kept and when training stops. A natural requirement on that metric is superiority: every correctly classified forecast should score better than every incorrectly classified one, however close the underlying probabilities are. Neither the Brier score nor the logarithmic score satisfies this on its own. We show that superiority is governed by the separation between two endpoints -- the supremum of the score on correct predictions and the infimum on incorrect predictions -- and derive both in closed form for each score. Their difference is the infimal penalty, the greatest lower bound on the penalty needed to restore superiority. Prior work restores superiority with a penalty calibrated from the first endpoint alone; for the Brier base, our infimal penalty is smaller than that published penalty by a factor ranging from 4.00 at three classes to 2.11 at twenty. We further embed the published and infimal penalties in a one-parameter family and show that, under a single-valued tie convention, every member of the family is strictly proper. In a pre-specified two-dataset case study, mean selected-model macro-F1 rises with the penalty in the reported ten-class regimes, though not distinguishably from noise once seed/selection-mode nesting is accounted for; a fifth regime at forty-seven classes does not reproduce even this descriptive pattern. The intended no-superiority baseline is algebraically a rescaling of the family under test, so the experiment cannot attribute the observed pattern specifically to superiority. When superiority itself is the objective, any penalty strictly above the infimal value suffices; choosing a larger penalty is a separate calibration trade-off rather than a requirement for the guarantee.
author: Rouhollah Ahmadian

title: SSPE: Robust Sequential Staypoint Extraction in Degraded Trajectory Data
content:
arXiv:2611.03737v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.
author: Yueyang Liu, Lance Kennedy, Andreas Z\"ufle

title: RATSIFT: Resolution-Adaptive Transformer for Solar Irradiance Forecasting and Temporal Downscaling
content:
arXiv:2611.03738v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Accurate forecasting and temporal downscaling of solar irradiance is critical for reliable renewable energy integration and grid management. Traditional methods often struggle to capture rapid irradiance variability. In this work, we develop a Transformer-based architecture for simultaneous forecasting and temporal downscaling. The model takes input data at arbitrary resolutions and generates outputs at any resolutions represented within the training data, leveraging both global and local contextual information. To improve training efficiency, a genetic algorithm-based optimization framework is implemented to identify suitable model hyperparameters, while reducing the computational cost of exhaustive grid search. The effectiveness of the proposed model is shown by analyzing real data in Dallas, Texas. The proposed model achieved root mean square error (RMSE) values of 28.785, 29.544, 30.157, 32.132~W/m\(^2\) for 15-, 30-, 60-minute, and irregularly spaced global input and producing forecast at 5-minutes resolution, respectively. Furthermore, this model produced reliable uncertainty estimates, exhibiting wider prediction intervals for high-resolution inputs during volatile solar conditions, whereas coarser-resolution inputs result in narrower intervals and significantly lower training time and computational cost. Our approach provides a scalable and efficient framework for multi-resolution solar irradiance forecasting and temporal downscaling, suitable for practical energy forecasting and grid management applications.
author: Jesto Peter, Timothy M. Hansen, Hossein Moradi Rekabdarkolaee

title: CaRe-KT: Continuity-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning for Knowledge Tracing
content:
arXiv:2611.03744v1 Announce Type: new
